Among 498 extracorporeal membrane oxygenation procedures, 218 infarct-related cardiogenic shock cases were identified. After excluding 76 extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation cases, 142 patients were analysed. Post-support pathways were classified as recovery surrogate, cardiac surgery, heart transplantation, durable left ventricular assist device support, or bridge failure. Cardiac surgery, heart transplantation, and durable left ventricular assist device support were combined as definitive downstream bridging. Exploratory multivariable logistic regression examined early characteristics associated with recovery surrogate versus bridge failure.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Mean age was 57.5 ± 11.5 years, and 112 patients (78.9%) were male. Mortality at 28, 90, and 365 days was 33.8%, 40.8%, and 41.5%, respectively. Recovery surrogate was reached in 68 patients (47.9%), bridge failure occurred in 53 (37.3%), heart transplantation in 14 (9.9%), cardiac surgery in 5 (3.5%), and durable left ventricular assist device support in 2 (1.4%). Overall, 21 patients (14.8%) entered definitive downstream bridging. Older age and out-of-hospital cannulation were associated with lower odds of definitive downstream bridging. Among the 121 patients without definitive downstream bridging, higher left ventricular ejection fraction, younger age and lower creatinine were associated with recovery surrogate in multivariable analysis. In exploratory adjusted survival analysis, definitive downstream bridging was associated with lower 365-day mortality.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Post-support pathways were heterogeneous. A pathway-based framework may better capture the clinical value of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation than mortality alone.

articles.title: Antibiotic utilization patterns, direct antibiotic acquisition costs, and hospital transfer outcomes in a pediatric emergency care unit: a retrospective study from Northeastern Brazil.
articles.journal_full: Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Antibiotic prescribing in pediatric emergency care represents an important clinical and economic challenge, particularly for antimicrobial stewardship and resource allocation. Evidence from pediatric emergency settings in low- and middle-income countries remains limited.

abstract.label: APPROACH
abstract.text: This retrospective study evaluated antibiotic prescribing patterns, direct antibiotic acquisition costs, and hospital-transfer status in a pediatric emergency care unit in Northeastern Brazil from 2019 to 2021. The full prescription dataset was used for descriptive analyses and cumulative acquisition cost estimation, whereas complete-case subsets were used for antibiotic unit-cost comparisons and hospital-transfer analyses. Direct costs were estimated using institutional acquisition prices. Statistical analyses included group comparisons, principal component analysis (PCA), and hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The descriptive sample comprised 10,489 antibiotic prescription records, with 324 treatment episodes included in the unit-cost analysis and 302 in the hospital-transfer analysis. The estimated minimum cumulative direct antibiotic acquisition cost for the overall prescription dataset was USD 13,044.67, with benzathine benzylpenicillin, ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, and azithromycin accounting for the highest cumulative costs. Antibiotic unit costs differed significantly across diagnostic groups (p = 0.022). Among treatment episodes included in the unit-cost analysis, 78.1% of antibiotics were classified as Access and 21.9% as Watch according to the World Health Organization (WHO) Access, Watch, and Reserve (AWaRe) classification, with no Reserve antibiotics identified. Exploratory PCA and HCA showed differences in therapeutic profiles across diagnostic groups. Higher antibiotic unit costs were observed among transferred episodes, although only seven episodes involved transfer, limiting the interpretation of this exploratory comparison.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Antibiotic utilization and direct antibiotic acquisition costs varied across pediatric diagnoses, highlighting opportunities for antimicrobial stewardship and pharmaceutical resource optimization in pediatric emergency care.

articles.title: The Knowledge-Practice Gap in Pharmacists' Management of Suspected Meningococcal Disease During Mass Gatherings: Evidence from Surveys and Simulated Patient Visits.

abstract.text: Background: Meningococcal disease remains a public health concern during mass gatherings such as Hajj and Umrah, where crowding, close contact, and travel may increase transmission risk. Although pharmacists play a role in prevention and early referral, existing studies have relied on self-reported assessments, which may not reflect actual practice. Aim: To assess pharmacists' knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported practices regarding the recognition, referral, and preventive management of suspected meningococcal disease during mass gatherings, and to compare reported practices with community pharmacists' behavior observed during simulated patient encounters at the group level. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted from February to June 2026 in Makkah, Jeddah, Madinah, and Taif. A total of 380 community and hospital pharmacists completed a questionnaire assessing knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported practices regarding post-exposure meningococcal prevention. In parallel, 305 simulated patient visits assessed practice among community pharmacists using a standardized scenario. Spearman correlation, multivariable linear regression with robust standard errors, and chi-squared or Fisher's exact tests (with Holm adjustment for regional comparisons) were used for analysis. Results: Pharmacists demonstrated good knowledge (median score, 5.0/6), attitudes (median, 13.0/15), and favorable self-reported practices (median, 15.5/20). However, only 5.2% of simulated patient encounters resulted in recognition of meningococcal disease, 7.5% included enquiry about close contact, and 6.2% included preventive counselling. Immediate referral was observed in 30.5% of encounters, while 88.9% involved symptomatic medication provision. Knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported practices were positively correlated with one another (Spearman's rho = 0.32-0.54). Conclusions: A substantial group-level gap was observed between favorable self-reported practices and lower performance in a separate, unlinked sample of community pharmacists. Practical, case-based education, standardized referral pathways, and simulation-based training may help improve pharmacists' ability to recognize and manage meningococcal disease during mass gatherings.

articles.title: Madrid Nurses' Perceptions, Needs, and Expectations Regarding Extended Reality-Based Resilience Training: A Multicenter Qualitative Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Nurses routinely work under substantial emotional and organizational demands that may challenge their professional well-being and capacity to respond to stressful clinical situations. Resilience training may support healthcare professionals in managing these demands, while Extended Reality (XR) offers opportunities to recreate emotionally and clinically relevant situations within controlled learning environments.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To explore nurses' perceptions, needs, and expectations regarding XR-based resilience training and to identify the organizational, professional, and technological conditions that may shape its future implementation.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A multicenter qualitative descriptive-interpretive study was conducted between February and March 2025 across three hospitals and one out-of-hospital emergency medical service in Madrid, Spain. Twenty-six nurses participated in four focus groups. Following open recruitment, participants were purposively selected according to professional profiles to obtain variation in professional experience and clinical settings. Data were analyzed inductively using open coding, constant comparison, progressive category development, analytic memos, and examination of relationships among categories. These procedures were informed by Grounded Theory analytical strategies but were not used to claim a full Grounded Theory methodology. Three researchers independently participated in qualitative coding, and interpretive differences were discussed through consensus. A researcher-developed AI-assisted qualitative analysis tool was used as a complementary resource for corpus exploration, while category development and conceptual interpretation remained researcher-led.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Three interrelated categories were identified: expectations regarding XR, perceived barriers, and facilitators and opportunities. Their relationships converged in an interpretive pattern of conditioned openness toward XR. Participants perceived immersive resilience training as potentially valuable when it was realistic, clinically relevant, and provided a safe environment for experiential learning and reflection. However, willingness to engage with XR was constrained by workload, limited training time, technological concerns, and organizational conditions. Protected training time, institutional support, supportive leadership, technical assistance, and professional participation in scenario design emerged as enabling conditions.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Participants perceived XR as a potentially useful approach to resilience training, but their openness to its implementation was conditional on clinical relevance and organizational feasibility. The findings do not establish the effectiveness of XR in improving resilience. Rather, they identify professional, organizational, and technological conditions that should inform the participatory design and future evaluation of XR-based resilience interventions.

articles.title: From Anatomy to Pathology: How Well Can AI Interpret Static Point-of-Care Ultrasound Images?

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Multimodal artificial intelligence may support point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) interpretation in emergency medicine, but its performance on static images and sensitivity to acquisition context remain uncertain. This study evaluated GPT-5.6 Sol and assessed whether probe-region information improves interpretation across view/plane, anatomy, and pathology domains. Methods: In this paired comparative in silico study, 92 educational ultrasound images from seven anatomical regions were assessed under standardized uninformed (image only) and informed (image plus probe-region code) prompting conditions. Two independent raters scored responses against textbook-based references in three domains: view/plane identification, anatomical structure identification, and pathological finding detection. Each domain was scored from 0 to 2. Disagreements were resolved by a third ultrasound expert, and fully correct responses were defined as domain scores of 2. The primary outcome was the total performance score (0-6). Secondary outcomes included domain-specific scores, fully correct response rates, and exploratory subgroup analyses. Wilcoxon signed-rank and McNemar tests assessed paired scores and fully correct rates, respectively. Results: Total performance was higher with informed prompting (median (interquartile range), 5 (4-6) versus 4 (2-5); p < 0.001). Interrater agreement was substantial to almost perfect across evaluation domains (quadratic-weighted κ = 0.750-1.000). Fully correct rates increased from 58.7% to 88.0% for view/plane identification and from 47.8% to 82.6% for anatomical structure identification (both p < 0.001). Pathological finding detection improved from 35.9% to 48.9% (p = 0.002). Among pathology-positive images, missed or incorrectly labeled pathology remained frequent (44.8%) despite informed prompting. Regional differences in total performance were significant only under uninformed prompting (p = 0.002). Conclusions: Probe-region information substantially improved view/plane and anatomical structure identification, but pathological finding detection remained comparatively weak. In static POCUS interpretation, improved anatomical recognition did not translate into reliable pathology detection. Persistent false-negative and false-positive errors do not support independent diagnostic use. Potential applications in POCUS education and anatomical labeling require further validation.

articles.title: Recovery trajectories of dizziness-related symptom burden and their associations with functional recovery and adverse post-discharge outcomes in older adults with ischemic vertigo: a prospective longitudinal study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Recovery after ischemic vertigo in older adults is heterogeneous, but longitudinal patterns of dizziness-related symptom burden and their clinical correlates remain insufficiently characterized. We aimed to identify distinct symptom-recovery trajectories, characterize functional recovery and adverse post-discharge outcomes across these trajectories, and examine clinical factors associated with unfavorable trajectory membership.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a prospective longitudinal study of adults aged 65 years or older with confirmed ischemic vertigo who were recruited between February and December 2025 and followed for 6 months after discharge. Dizziness-related symptom burden was assessed using the Dizziness Handicap Inventory at discharge baseline, 7 days, 1 month, 3 months, and 6 months. Latent class growth analysis was used to identify distinct symptom-recovery trajectories. Functional recovery, falls or near-falls, and healthcare reutilization were compared across the identified classes. All enrolled participants contributed available repeated measurements through full-information maximum likelihood, and factors associated with unfavorable class membership were examined using a three-step approach that accounted for classification uncertainty.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 231 enrolled participants, 214 completed at least three follow-up assessments and 189 completed all scheduled assessments; all 231 contributed available data to the trajectory analysis. A three-class solution was identified: favorable recovery (118 participants, 51.1%), intermediate recovery (74 participants, 32.0%), and unfavorable recovery (39 participants, 16.9%). Compared with the favorable class, the unfavorable class showed persistently higher dizziness-related handicap, slower Barthel Index improvement, lower recovery to pre-morbid mobility, and higher frequencies of emergency-department revisits and falls or near-falls. Prior stroke or transient ischemic attack, mobility limitation at discharge, and NIHSS score ≥3 were associated with unfavorable trajectory membership.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Recovery after emergency-department management of ischemic vertigo in older adults is heterogeneous. Early clinical features and recovery patterns were associated with persistent symptom burden, delayed functional recovery, and adverse post-discharge outcomes. Their potential role in guiding individualized follow-up and transitional care should be evaluated prospectively.

articles.title: The Clinical Phenotype of Green Pit Viper (Trimeresurus spp.) Envenomation: A Comprehensive Review.

abstract.text: Green pit vipers of the genus Trimeresurus are among the leading causes of snakebite envenomation across tropical and subtropical Asia, yet their clinical phenotype has been less systematically characterized than that of other medically important Asian viperids. This comprehensive review synthesizes the published clinical literature on human Trimeresurus envenomation, drawing on 70 clinical reports encompassing 4720 reported patient episodes, and integrates these data with current taxonomic and venomic evidence. Envenomations cluster in East, Southeast, and South Asia. The single most important limitation of this literature is the unreliability of species attribution: 55% of reported cases are attributed only at genus level or derive from cohorts in which two or more Trimeresurus species are reported together and cannot be separated, a figure consistent with the 56% of snakebites left unidentified in a recent 40,817-patient Chinese survey. Bites involve the extremities almost exclusively, with a predominance of the lower limb (55% versus 45%). The clinical picture is dominated by local effects (i.e., extensive edema and pain in the large majority of patients, secondary infection in approximately one in six, and cutaneous necrosis in approximately one in thirty) and by systemic hemotoxicity driven by venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy. Renal involvement is uncommon, in contrast to Daboia russelii envenomation, and severe neurotoxicity is exceptional. Documented mortality in the reviewed hospital-based literature is low (two deaths among 3387 patients in reports documenting outcome, <0.1%) but is not zero, and hospital-based series cannot capture pre-hospital deaths. Management centers on conservative wound care, serial coagulation monitoring, and selective antivenom administration; routine fasciotomy is not justified without objective evidence of compartment syndrome. Reliable species identification, standardized clinical reporting, and long-term functional follow-up remain the principal unmet needs.

articles.title: Metabolically Controlled Oncological Treatment: An Evidence-Graded Framework Integrating Metabolic Reprogramming, Targeted Drug Delivery, and Standard Oncological Care.

abstract.text: Cancer cells exhibit metabolic reprogramming, including increased aerobic glycolysis, glutaminolysis, and altered lipid metabolism, which supports tumor growth and contributes to immune evasion. A growing but heterogeneous body of literature has investigated whether targeting these metabolic dependencies alongside standard oncologic treatment may provide therapeutic benefit. This review critically examines clinically investigated metabolically directed approaches, including metronomic chemotherapy, hyperthermia, high-dose intravenous vitamin C, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, fasting-related nutritional strategies, ketogenic diets, and insulin-based approaches, while distinguishing them from established targeted therapies, monoclonal antibodies, and immune checkpoint inhibitors. Emerging immunometabolic and microenvironmental targets are also discussed, including lactate transport, ferroptosis, autophagy and amino acid metabolism, cancer-associated fibroblasts, tumor-associated macrophages, abnormal vasculature, and immunosuppressive cytokine signaling. In addition, drug-delivery strategies are considered by distinguishing the established pharmaceutical role of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as a solvent or excipient from nanoparticle-, exosome-, and peptide-based targeting platforms. Available evidence is characterized according to clinical maturity, ranging from established phase III-supported therapies and randomized clinical evidence to early-phase, preclinical, or currently unproven approaches. Although several metabolically directed interventions have biological rationale and varying degrees of clinical support, no comprehensive multicomponent metabolic regimen has been validated in controlled clinical trials. Future development should prioritize stepwise, biomarker-informed prospective studies evaluating individual interventions and biologically justified combinations alongside standard-of-care therapy. Metabolically directed strategies should therefore be interpreted according to the evidence supporting each component rather than as a single established therapeutic regimen.

articles.title: A Spatial Decision-Support Framework for Assessing Road Network Efficiency in Emergency Healthcare Accessibility: A Case Study of Eastern Province Cities, Saudi Arabia.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The pressure on emergency medical services (EMSs) has been exacerbated by increased urbanization and population growth in major Saudi cities such as Dammam, Al Khobar, and Dhahran. In this study, a spatial decision-support framework is proposed to determine the accessibility to ambulance services and hospitals.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Within the spatial decision-support framework, modeled two-leg travel time (station-to-scene plus scene-to-hospital, including modeled traffic-signal delays) is evaluated under both peak and non-peak traffic conditions, using a 30 min travel-time threshold. The model comprises road network data, ambulance and hospital locations, and traffic conditions to evaluate the travel component of emergency healthcare accessibility and to identify areas that are disadvantaged. Times for dispatch, ambulance response, scene assessment and treatment, stabilization, and loading are not included.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The results reveal significant spatial and temporal disparities, with accessibility decreasing during peak hours. Al Khobar has relatively better accessibility, while Dammam is consistently and significantly underserved, and Dhahran has moderate access. Taking into account the population data, it is evident that unequal accessibility is due to both spatial and demographic factors, with a significant number of residents having poor access to EMS.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The findings can inform the improvement of EMS planning and people's access to equitable healthcare. The framework can support the connection of underserved areas and direct development in the spatial distribution of emergency healthcare services.

articles.title: [Organised de-shock: greater efficiency for improved safety].

abstract.text: A child's condition in the paediatric emergency department can deteriorate rapidly, requiring immediate care in the critical care unit. This situation causes stress for healthcare staff, as they must act quickly whilst drawing on specific skills and demonstrating good organisational skills. The reorganisation of this unit, centred on signage using specific colours, and the creation of care kits have led to improvements in safety, speed and efficiency.

articles.title: Bystander CPR Type and Outcomes After Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: Compression-only cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CO-CPR) has been widely promoted to encourage bystander intervention in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but long-term trends in bystander CPR and the associations between CPR type and outcomes in pediatric OHCA remain unclear.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate temporal trends in bystander CPR type and the associations with clinical outcomes among children with OHCA in Japan.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This cohort study included patients aged 17 years or younger with known receipt of bystander CPR documented in the nationwide All-Japan Utstein Registry from January 1, 2005, to December 31, 2023. Data analysis was performed from November 24, 2025, to September 2, 2026, including additional analyses conducted during the revision process.

abstract.label: EXPOSURES
abstract.text: Bystander CPR was categorized as rescue-breathing CPR (RB-CPR), CO-CPR, or no bystander CPR.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
abstract.text: The primary outcome was 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate; secondary outcomes were 30-day survival rate and prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Temporal trends were assessed with multinomial logistic regression, and associations between CPR type and outcomes were evaluated using modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation, with CO-CPR serving as the reference.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 26 785 pediatric patients with OHCA (median [IQR] age, 2.0 [0-12] years; 16 254 males [60.7%]), 6543 (24.4%) received RB-CPR, 9112 (34.0%) received CO-CPR, and 11 130 (41.6%) received no bystander CPR. The adjusted probability of CO-CPR increased from 14.6% (95% CI, 13.1%-16.1%) in 2005 to 55.1% (95% CI, 52.5%-57.6%) in 2023, whereas RB-CPR declined from 41.7% (95% CI, 39.7%-43.7%) to 10.4% (95% CI, 8.7%-12.1%). The adjusted probability of receiving no bystander CPR plateaued at approximately 35.0% after 2013. Neurologically favorable 30-day survival rate occurred in 3.6% receiving no bystander CPR, 9.5% receiving CO-CPR, and 16.0% receiving RB-CPR. Compared with CO-CPR, RB-CPR was associated with a higher 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 1.71; 95% CI, 1.57-1.86), 30-day survival rate (ARR, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.42-1.61), and prehospital ROSC (ARR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.51-1.75), whereas receipt of no bystander CPR was associated with lower probabilities of these outcomes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: In this cohort study of children with OHCA, increasing CO-CPR use coincided with declining RB-CPR but not with further reductions in untreated arrests after 2013. No bystander CPR was associated with worse outcomes compared with CO-CPR and RB-CPR. RB-CPR had more favorable outcomes than CO-CPR, supporting the continued importance of rescue breathing in pediatric resuscitation.

articles.title: Timing of Antenatal Care, Stillbirth, and Infant Mortality in Migrant Mothers in Australia.

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: Timely antenatal care (ANC) reduces pregnancy risks, yet the association between delayed ANC and stillbirth or infant mortality among migrant mothers in Australia has not previously been investigated.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To examine whether delayed ANC is associated with higher stillbirth and infant mortality among Australia-born compared with migrant mothers.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort study assessed births to non-Indigenous mothers in New South Wales from January 1, 2002, to December 31, 2020, followed up to infant age of 1 year. Mothers were categorized as Australia-born, migrant from English-speaking country (ESM), or migrant from non-English-speaking country (non-ESM). Data were analyzed between August 2025 and June 2026.

abstract.label: EXPOSURES
abstract.text: Timing of first ANC, defined as 12 weeks or earlier, 13 to 19 weeks, 20 weeks or later, or no ANC.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
abstract.text: The main outcome was stillbirth (at ≥20 weeks) and infant mortality (at prehospital discharge, posthospital discharge, or 1 year). Adjusted relative risks (ARRs) were estimated using Poisson regression models, stratified by migration group.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: This study included 1 720 033 births (median [IQR] maternal age, 31.2 [27.4-34.8] years; 884 235 male infants [51.4%]), including 1 132 193 (65.8%) to Australia-born, 116 026 (6.7%) to ESM, and 471 814 (27.4%) to non-ESM mothers. Late ANC (>12 weeks) was more common in non-ESM mothers (190 338 [40.3%]) than Australia-born (334 790 [29.6%]) or ESM (41 029 [35.4%]) mothers. In cross-group comparisons, non-ESM mother status was associated with higher risk of adverse outcomes regardless of ANC timing. Compared with Australia-born mothers with early ANC (≤12 weeks), a higher risk of stillbirth (ARR, 1.25; 95% CI, 1.18-1.33) and 1-year (ARR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.22-1.44), predischarge (ARR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.25-1.54), and postdischarge (ARR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.03-1.37) infant mortality was observed in non-ESM mothers accessing ANC by 12 weeks. Similar risk patterns were observed in non-ESM mothers with late ANC. In within-group comparisons, among Australia-born mothers, each category of delayed ANC was associated with higher risk. No ANC was associated with the highest risks across all maternal groups for stillbirth and 1-year infant mortality. For non-ESM mothers, late ANC (≥20 weeks) was associated with a lower risk of predischarge mortality (ARR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.61-0.92) but a higher risk of postdischarge mortality (ARR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.02-1.65).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: In this cohort study of 1.72 million births, higher risks of stillbirths and infant mortalities were observed in non-ESM mothers regardless of ANC timing, warranting further investigation.

articles.title: Occupational heat stress in nurses working in hot environments and wearing personal protective equipment: mechanisms, health and safety implications, and prevention.

abstract.text: Climate change is increasing the frequency, intensity, and duration of extreme heat, while infection prevention and other clinical demands require many nurses to work in personal protective equipment (PPE). Hot environments and PPE use can coexist in emergency departments, intensive care units, infectious disease wards, operating rooms, prehospital services, and other settings in which workload, restricted recovery opportunities, and limited access to hydration may compound thermal strain. This narrative review integrates current evidence on the pathways through which environmental heat, metabolic workload, and PPE-related resistance to heat loss may affect nurses and other healthcare workers. An initial set of 31 references identified by the authors was updated through a PubMed search conducted on 2 September 2026 (three queries covering January 2024 to September 2026, plus one calibration query without date limits). For each cited study, the population, design, main findings, and directness to nurses were extracted, and the evidence was synthesized narratively across four domains: pathways, health and safety implications, risk assessment and monitoring, and prevention. Available studies, mostly of mixed healthcare-worker populations, consistently describe thermal discomfort, sweating, thirst, fatigue, headache, dizziness, and impaired well-being among PPE-exposed healthcare workers; however, nurse-specific longitudinal evidence and direct evidence linking heat strain to occupational injuries or patient-safety events remain limited. Effective prevention therefore requires more than individual coping. Healthcare facilities should combine environmental surveillance, task and PPE-sensitive risk assessment, accessible hydration and cooled recovery areas, work-rest and staffing arrangements, risk-appropriate PPE, personal cooling where feasible, symptom reporting, and emergency response. Future research should prioritize nurse-specific prospective cohorts, standardized exposure and outcome measures that include nurses' well-being and occupational safety, field-based intervention studies, and implementation outcomes across diverse climates and clinical settings. Integrating occupational heat protection into climate-resilient health-system planning may protect both the nursing workforce and continuity of care.

articles.title: Case Report: Raw grass carp gallbladder ingestion and acute liver injury.

abstract.text: Raw grass carp gallbladder ingestion for folk medicinal purposes may cause severe acute liver injury driven by the hepatotoxin 5α-cyprinol sulfate, yet high-dose human poisoning cases remain infrequently documented. We report a 60-year-old male (60 kg body weight) who developed severe intoxication 22 h after consuming six raw gallbladders from grass carps of approximately 1.5 kg each. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea occurred within 2 hours of ingestion. Laboratory testing on admission demonstrated extreme hepatocellular injury (ALT 6285 U/L, AST 9321 U/L). Conventional hepatoprotective agents plus pre-hospital haemoperfusion yielded limited biochemical improvement. While admitted to the intensive care unit, the patient received one session of double plasma molecular adsorption system, three sessions of plasma exchange and four sessions of continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT, CVVHDF modality) alongside comprehensive supportive care. Liver function normalized within 14 hospital days; no acute kidney injury was observed. Complete symptomatic recovery was documented at the 4-week follow-up visit, though longer-term outcomes remain unknown given the limited follow-up duration. Toxin-mediated hepatocyte damage is partially supported by pre-clinical cyprinol-sulfate experimental work; many downstream oxidative, mitochondrial, endoplasmic-reticulum and inflammatory molecular pathways remain hypothetical and are largely extrapolated from unrelated liver-injury models, without direct validation in human carp-gallbladder-poisoning tissue specimens. Biochemical improvement was temporally associated with multimodal extracorporeal purification, but causal therapeutic benefit can't be proven from this uncontrolled single case; spontaneous hepatic regeneration may also contribute to recovery. This case highlights substantial hazards associated with folk-health beliefs promoting raw fish-gallbladder consumption, emphasising the need for early clinical recognition of fish-gallbladder poisoning.

articles.title: Sudden Deaths From Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and Proximity to Neurosurgical Tertiary Care.

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: A substantial proportion of deaths due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) occur without admission to neurosurgical units. Whether this proportion varies by geographic region is unclear.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To determine the proportion of SAH deaths without neurosurgical unit admission across hospital districts in 2 high-income countries.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This retrospective, population-based cohort study used 2 externally validated nationwide administrative data collections in all 41 hospital districts and 10 neurosurgical units in Finland and New Zealand from January 1, 2001, to December 31, 2017. Participants included all hospitalized and fatal nonhospitalized cases with SAH. Data were analyzed from July 1, 2024, to September 7, 2026.

abstract.label: EXPOSURES
abstract.text: Hospital district of residence and its distance to the designated neurosurgical referral center, grouped into 4 zones.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
abstract.text: The primary outcome was the death-based proportion of all 30-day deaths after SAH that occurred without neurosurgical unit admission (prehospital deaths plus deaths within 30 days after admission to a nonneurosurgical unit divided by all 30-day deaths from SAH). This proportion was estimated across 41 hospital districts and demographic groups, with age- and sex-adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and 95% CIs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 12 912 patients with SAH (7856 in Finland and 5056 in New Zealand; median age, 58 [IQR, 49-69] years; 7924 [61.4%] women) were included. Of all 5418 SAH deaths, 3819 (70.5%) occurred without neurosurgical unit admission: 2203 of 3114 (70.7%) in Finland (interdistrict range, 403 of 644 [62.6%] to 5 of 5 [100%]) and 1616 of 2304 (70.1%) in New Zealand (interdistrict range, 111 of 190 [58.4%] to 22 of 23 [95.7%]). Compared with districts containing a neurosurgical unit (1723 of 2602 [66.2%]), the death-based proportions were higher in close-distance (1-130 km; 796 of 1129 [70.5%]; RR, 1.07 [95% CI, 1.02-1.12]), middle-distance (131-157 km; 469 of 599 [78.3%]; RR, 1.18 [95% CI, 1.12-1.24]), and far-distance (158-371 km; 831 of 1088 [76.4%]; RR, 1.15 [95% CI, 1.10-1.20]) zones. This proportion increased by 6.7% (95% CI, 4.9%-8.5%) for each additional 100 km to a neurosurgical unit. The proportions decreased in both countries over time.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: In this cohort study of 12 912 patients with SAH, most deaths occurred without neurosurgical unit admission, and this proportion increased with distance to the neurosurgical referral center. Prevention and early management outside tertiary care may therefore warrant priority in reducing SAH mortality.

articles.title: Climate Vulnerability, Historical Redlining, and Children's Mental Health Care Use.

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: Structural inequities stemming from historical redlining and environmental injustice have created varying levels of risk among marginalized communities. However, the association of climate risk and structural racism with pediatric mental health care use remains underexplored.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To examine associations between climate vulnerability and pediatric mental health care use, and to assess whether these associations vary by historical redlining status.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This cross-sectional study of children aged younger than 18 years residing in New York State between 2017 and 2022 used all-payer hospital administrative data from the New York State Department of Health. Statistical analysis was conducted from January 2025 through February 2026.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOME AND MEASURES
abstract.text: Outcomes included mental health-related emergency department (ED) and outpatient visits identified using International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision-coded mental health diagnosis subtypes (eg, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), aggregated at the census-tract level. The primary exposure was climate-specific Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles (where 1 indicates low climate vulnerability and 4 indicates high climate vulnerability). Poisson regression models were conducted to examine associations between Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles and mental health-related health care utilization, including interactions with neighborhood-level redlining status (Home Owners' Loan Corporation grades C/D vs A/B) and subtype-specific analyses. Models adjusted for age, sex, self- or guardian-reported race and ethnicity, and neighborhood-level covariates, with coefficients reported as rate ratios (RRs).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 553 134 mental health-related visits were included (mean [SD] age, 7.2 [5.8] years; 285 526 male [51.6%]). Compared with children living in areas with the lowest climate vulnerability, those living in the highest-vulnerability areas had higher outpatient visit rates (RR, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.72-2.27) and non-statistically significantly higher ED visit rates (RR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.96-1.35). Associations between high climate vulnerability and mental health-related health care utilization varied by redlining status. In historically redlined neighborhoods, high climate vulnerability was associated with outpatient health care utilization (RR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.44-1.51; P < .001 for interaction) and, to a lesser extent, ED utilization (RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.09; P < .001 for interaction); in nonredlined neighborhoods high climate vulnerability was associated with lower outpatient health care utilization (RR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.45-0.49; P < .001 for interaction) and not associated with ED utilization (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.93-1.07). Associations also varied across mental health diagnosis subtypes, with higher climate vulnerability associated with increased health care utilization for most diagnosis subtypes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: In this cross-sectional study of children, residence in historically redlined and climate-vulnerable neighborhoods was associated with higher rates of mental health-related health care utilization. These findings highlight geographic patterns in mental health-related health care utilization that may be relevant to future research on climate preparedness, mental health services, culturally responsive care, and access to services for children experiencing climate-related stressors and structural inequities.

articles.title: Community Aftercare Linkage and Acute Clinical Outcomes Among Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department Following Suicide Attempts: A Retrospective Cohort Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This study examined factors associated with successful community aftercare linkage after emergency department (ED) presentation following suicide attempts, with acute hospital outcomes evaluated separately.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This single-center retrospective cohort included 1035 patients aged ≥ 15 years presenting during 2023-2025. Successful linkage was defined as confirmed initial registration at a community mental health center. Multivariable logistic regression assessed linkage among 975 discharge survivors; intensive care unit (ICU) admission and in-hospital mortality were secondary outcomes in the full cohort.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among survivors, 530 (54.4%) accepted hospital-based case management and 213 (21.8%) achieved linkage, representing 40.2% of accepting survivors. College attendance (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.69; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.12-2.55), psychiatric history (aOR, 1.69; 95% CI, 1.13-2.55), and previous suicide attempts (aOR, 1.81; 95% CI, 1.27-2.56) were associated with linkage. The intubation estimate was uncertain (aOR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.26-1.06). Model discrimination was modest (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.710), with evidence of lack of fit (Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.009). ICU admission occurred in 218 patients (21.1%) and in-hospital death in 60 (5.8%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Initial acceptance and completed linkage were distinct stages of this care pathway. The associated factors may inform further investigation of care transitions, but initial registration does not establish sustained treatment engagement.

articles.title: Caring for Patients Anywhere, Anyhow: How Emergency Department Crowding and Boarding Shapes Professional Identity in Emergency Medicine Training.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency department (ED) boarding is a well-documented crisis associated with adverse patient outcomes, healthcare worker burnout, and moral injury. Although prior work has documented operational and educational impacts, including reductions in resident productivity and procedural exposure, less is known about how sustained boarding shapes professional identity formation. We sought to explore how sustained ED boarding shapes the learning experiences and professional identity formation of emergency medicine (EM) residents, as perceived by both residents and the attending physicians who train them.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Using a constructivist paradigm, we conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with residents and attending physicians from a 4-year EM residency program with rotations across 5 clinical sites, between July and August 2025. Two researchers independently coded transcripts and iteratively refined a shared codebook, continuing until additional interviews were unlikely to add new insight, guided by the concept of information power. We used reflexive thematic analysis, treating researchers' clinical and analytic judgment as a resource for identifying patterns of meaning, and prioritized participants' own construction of meaning over the frequency of any single idea, consistent with an interpretive phenomenological approach.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We interviewed 13 emergency physicians: 6 residents and 7 attending physicians (range: 1-30+ years after residency). Three overarching themes emerged: (1) Educational challenges and opportunities-boarding fragments diagnostic ownership, narrows the acuity spectrum, and limits authentic undifferentiated encounters, although attending physicians adapt through structured hypotheticals and micro-teaching); (2) Shifts in the clinical environment-operational and structural adaptations create educational dead space, constrain the therapeutic alliance, and generate role ambiguity around boarded patients); and (3) Moral strain and suffering-moral injury and combined suffering is not peripheral to training but embedded within it, shaping how residents interpret professional responsibility and integrity. The three themes exist in a triangular relationship, with suffering at the foundation.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Boarding appeared to function as a formative context for professional identity formation, not merely a disruptive one. Residents described learning systems-level practice, advocacy, and emotional regulation, often through loss and moral injury, alongside attending physicians navigating the same. These findings suggest that recognizing boarding as a structural condition of training may reorient the responsibility of graduate medical education: formalizing adaptive teaching strategies, creating structured opportunities to process moral strain, and committing to advocacy that treats boarding as the educational crisis it is.

articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

articles.title: Off Service, with Purpose: Creating Learner-Centered Experiences for Off-Service Residents.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.text: Academic emergency departments (EDs) host off-service residents (OSRs) from various specialties. While OSRs contribute meaningfully to patient care, they often face unique challenges during their ED rotations, including limited preparation, heightened stress, and unmet personal expectations. Despite a standardized curriculum endorsed by the American College of Emergency Physicians, guidance on how to foster meaningful educational experiences for OSRs remains sparse. This perspective offers a structured approach grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), which emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as essential to intrinsic motivation and effective learning. By aligning educational strategies with SDT principles, emergency medicine educators can enhance engagement, support learner development, and create lasting interprofessional collaboration. Ultimately, this learner-centered approach not only enriches the OSR experience but also strengthens the role of the ED as a dynamic, inclusive learning environment for all trainees.

articles.title: Anticipating Change: Local Attitudes Toward a New Community Emergency Medicine Residency Program.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The Indiana University School of Medicine launched two new community-based residency programs at Indiana University Health Bloomington (IUH-B) in July 2026. Prior to the launch, this research explored community members' attitudes, expectations, and concerns regarding the introduction of resident physicians to the emergency department (ED).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This study was conducted from June to July 2025 at IUH-B. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, we evaluated a convenience sample of adult patients and accompanying family members in the emergency department (ED). Data collection included a 16-item electronic survey and semi-structured interviews.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The survey was completed by 39 adult participants, and 40 completed the qualitative interview. Most participants (59%) were aware of the residency programs, and nearly all (95%) agreed that residents would improve the quality, access, and modernity of healthcare in Bloomington, with very few expressing concerns about resident involvement. Overall, 97% of respondents stated support for the expansion of additional physician training programs locally. Comfort with or support for residency programs was not significantly influenced by prior experience with residents or awareness of the new programs. Thematic analysis shows that participants value residents who are competent, personable, and attentive listeners, while emphasizing the importance of strong supervision by attending physicians. Overall, participants are optimistic that new residency programs will bring more clinicians and up-to-date medical practices to the Bloomington area.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Participants viewed the implementation of a new residency program positively, agreeing with proposed benefits and expressing minimal concerns. To ensure successful integration, further community initiatives should focus on educational outreach regarding the specific roles and training levels of emergency medicine residents, and prepare for implementation of trainees.

articles.title: A Case-Based Workshop to Enhance Leadership Self-Efficacy Among Women in Academic Emergency Medicine.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Women remain underrepresented in emergency medicine leadership roles, in part due to sex-based stereotypes that undervalue leadership traits traditionally associated with women, such as collaboration and empathy. Agentic traits like assertiveness are often perceived as requisite for leadership, while communal skills are overlooked. Leadership self-efficacy, an individual's belief in their ability to successfully perform leadership roles, is a key predictor of leadership emergence.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Our team developed a 90-minute didactic session featuring a panel of diverse women leaders followed by an interactive case-based exercise, delivered at the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine 35th Annual Meeting in 2024. The intervention was evaluated using a pre- and postsurvey based on an adapted Leadership Self-Efficacy Scale measuring six domains of leadership self-efficacy. Eighteen participants completed both the pre- and postsession surveys, providing 18 matched pre-post pairs for analysis. Participants rated their confidence on a seven-point Likert scale. Our outcome of interest was the change in mean self-efficacy score for each domain on this seven-point scale, assessed with paired t-tests.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: All six leadership domains showed increased mean scores postintervention. Dimension 1 (Leading Change) increased significantly (mean change +0.72/7, P = .001), as did Dimension 2 (Choosing team/Delegating) (mean change +0.61/7, P = .004). Dimensions 3-6 showed positive but nonsignificant trends.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This single-session intervention was associated with increased leadership self-efficacy, particularly in the domains of leading change and team-building. The combination of role model exposure and interactive case practice may be a useful approach for empowering women physicians. This innovation can be adapted for implementation at other academic institutions.

articles.title: Clinical Value of Procalcitonin and Sarcopenia Index in Evaluating Intra-Abdominal Infection in Trauma Patients.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The aim is to evaluate the predictive value of serum procalcitonin (PCT) and the sarcopenia index (SI) for intra-abdominal infection (IAI) during hospitalization in patients with abdominal trauma; to compare the discriminatory performance of single indicators versus their combination, and to conduct gender-stratified and clinical application assessments.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A single-center cohort study was conducted that included patients with abdominal trauma (n = 326) ad-mitted through the emergency department. PCT levels on days 1, 3, and 5 (denoted as PCT1, PCT3, and PCT5, respectively), and SI was calculated using creatinine (Cr) and cystatin C (CysC). The main outcome was IAI during hospitalization. ROC curves and DeLong's test were used to compare the discriminative ability of PCT at different time points. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed stratified by gender. A combined model and nomogram were developed based on PCT3 and 1/SI. Decision curve analysis (DCA) and calibration curves were applied to evaluate clinical net benefit and model consistency.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The IAI group had significantly higher PCT levels at all time points compared to the non-IAI group. PCT3 demonstrated the best discriminatory performance, and was significantly superior to PCT1 and PCT5. Baseline comparisons revealed gender differences in SI, with male patients having higher SI than females, while no significant gender differences were found for PCT3 or the proportion of IAI. In gender-stratified regression, PCT3 was a common independent predictor of IAI in both male and female patients, while SI was negatively correlated with IAI. The combined model (PCT3 + 1/SI) outperformed any single indicator in both male and female groups. DCA showed a stable net clinical benefit, and the model was well-calibrated. The nomogram could be used for individualized bedside risk assessment.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: PCT3 is the strongest single predictor of IAI, and SI is negatively correlated with IAI. Their combination further enhances predictive discrimination, offering clinical net benefit and good calibration. Effective prediction of IAI can be achieved using routine serological indicators from hospital day 3 - serum PCT and SI calculated from routine Cr and CysC.

articles.title: Clinical Comparator Dependence of Inflammatory and Hematologic Biomarker Discrimination for Sepsis: A Matched Retrospective Study Using MIMIC-IV Emergency Department Data.

abstract.text: Background: The diagnostic performance of sepsis biomarkers may vary according to the clinical comparator population. We evaluated 11 routinely available inflammatory and hematologic biomarkers in two matched diagnostic settings. Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study using linked MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-ED, and MIMIC-IV-Note data. Adult emergency department episodes were classified as sepsis, suspected infection without sepsis, or controls without suspected infection. Comparison-specific profile matching retained the same 525 sepsis episodes in both analyses, together with 214 controls without suspected infection and 315 episodes with suspected infection without sepsis. Biomarker discrimination was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) with DeLong inference. Results: Against controls without suspected infection, C-reactive protein (CRP) had the highest AUROC (0.786; 95% CI, 0.748-0.823), followed by absolute lymphocyte count (0.654; 0.613-0.696) and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR; 0.636; 0.594-0.677). Against suspected infection without sepsis, absolute lymphocyte count had the highest AUROC (0.677; 0.641-0.714), followed by NLR (0.626; 0.588-0.664), whereas CRP discrimination decreased to 0.555 (0.514-0.595). The cross-setting difference for CRP was 0.231 (95% CI, 0.183-0.278; Holm-adjusted p <0.001). Sensitivity analyses produced similar qualitative findings. Conclusions: Biomarker discrimination for sepsis varied according to the clinical comparator population, with the magnitude of cross-setting change differing across biomarkers. CRP showed the largest change, whereas absolute lymphocyte count retained modest discrimination in both settings. These findings emphasize the importance of interpreting biomarker performance within clinically relevant diagnostic contrasts.

articles.title: The Effect of the Prognostic Nutritional Index and Triglyceride-Glucose Index for Predicting Mortality in Patients with Stroke.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Stroke is an acute condition in which impaired cerebral perfusion causes focal or global neurological dysfunction. Serious complications are a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in patients with stroke. Malnutrition is common in this population, and nutritional markers, including the prognostic nutritional index (PNI), may be useful for early risk assessment of stroke-associated infections. Insulin resistance (IR) is also an emerging risk factor for stroke and has been associated with poor prognosis through various metabolic and inflammatory pathways. The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index has been proposed as a reliable surrogate marker of IR. Various biochemical and clinical parameters are used to assess prognosis in patients with stroke. We investigated the prognostic value of the TyG index and PNI for mortality and early mortality, defined as death within the first 30 days, in these patients. Methods: After application of the exclusion criteria, 415 patients with stroke were included. Demographic characteristics, including age and sex, and comorbidities were reviewed. Complete blood count, biochemical parameters, C-reactive protein, blood gas measurements, and lactate levels were recorded. Brain computed tomography and diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging findings were reviewed to classify patients into ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke subgroups. Patients were grouped as survivors or nonsurvivors, and deaths within the first 30 days were classified as early mortality. PNI and TyG index values were calculated using the following formulas: PNI = 10 × serum albumin (g/dL) + 0.005 × total lymphocyte count (cells/mm3); TyG index = ln [fasting triglycerides (mg/dL) × fasting blood glucose (mg/dL)/2]. Results: Of the 415 patients included, 389 (93.7%) had ischemic stroke and 26 (6.3%) had hemorrhagic stroke. The median age was 74 years (IQR, 65.0-81.0), and the sex distribution was balanced: 207 patients (49.9%) were women and 208 (50.1%) were men. The PNI was lower in nonsurvivors than in survivors in the overall stroke cohort (ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke combined; 40.86 ± 8.02 vs. 46.88 ± 6.85, p < 0.001), the ischemic stroke subgroup (41.12 ± 8.77 vs. 46.82 ± 6.83, p = 0.001), and the hemorrhagic stroke subgroup (39.79 ± 3.79 vs. 48.17 ± 7.32, p = 0.006). The PNI was also lower in patients who died within the first 30 days than in survivors in the overall cohort (41.86 ± 8.42 vs. 46.88 ± 6.85, p < 0.001), the ischemic stroke subgroup (42.46 ± 8.90 vs. 46.82 ± 6.83, p = 0.002), and the hemorrhagic stroke subgroup (38.60 ± 4.35 vs. 48.17 ± 7.32, p = 0.012). Conclusions: Biomarkers calculated using simple hematological parameters have a significant impact on mortality and early mortality in stroke patients (both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke). When we examined the effects of these TyG and PNI markers on mortality in stroke patients in our study, we observed that the PNI had a significant impact on mortality. Although our findings suggest that the PNI independently predicts mortality or could guide risk assessment in the emergency department, we consider this an exploratory observation, as stroke severity measures-such as the NIHSS-and relevant treatment data were not included in our analyses. However, we believe that single-point TyG values do not carry sufficient significance regarding mortality; therefore, future research should take into account cumulative, repeated TyG measurements obtained during patient follow-up.

articles.title: Dedicated Vertical Physician Pilot in a Rotational Patient Assignment Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency department (ED) vertical patient pathways (VPP) assign patients to a dedicated care area with chairs, avoiding the use of traditional ED beds. The effect of reassigning a dedicated vertical emergency physician (EP) onto an established rotational patient assignment (RPA) system, which prospectively assigns arriving patients to EP queues, is unknown. We sought to describe operational outcomes and staff satisfaction with trialing this role.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a single-center, hypothesis-generating exploratory pilot at a 56-bed tertiary-care ED in which one 8.75-hour EP shift on five Mondays was repurposed into an 8.75-hour dedicated VPP role within a chair-based vertical patient care area while the rotational patient assignment system remained in place; three prior comparable Mondays served as comparison. Primary outcome was discharged-patient ED length of stay (LOS); secondary outcomes included VPP upgrades to a bed, patient numbers seen by the dedicated shift, and staff satisfaction. We report descriptive analyses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We analyzed 529 discharged-patient encounters: 199 (37.6%) during the preintervention period and 330 (62.4%) during the postintervention period. Median ED LOS for discharged patients did not demonstrate a consistent directional change, decreasing by seven minutes (3.1%) in the overall ED (226 vs 219 minutes) and increasing by 18.5 minutes (13.0%) among patients initially evaluated via the VPP (142.5 vs 161 minutes). The dedicated VPP EP saw three more patients per shift (21.4%; median 17 vs 14), and VPP upgrades fell from 15/68 (22.1%) to 5/130 (3.8%). Timeliness and communication were rated favorably by 4/4 VPP physician respondents and 10/12 and 16/17 registered nurse/allied health respondents, respectively; 3/4 VPP physician respondents vs 1/29 non-VPP physician respondents supported continuing the model.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Reassigning an existing EP to a dedicated vertical EP role within an ongoing rotational patient assignment system was not accompanied by shortened discharged-patient length of stay. Fewer VPP upgrades and a modest increase in patients seen by the dedicated shift were observed, but patient selection and acuity limit interpretation. Staff reported favorable teamwork within the vertical space, whereas non-VPP physicians reported less manageable workloads and little support for continuing the model.

articles.title: Acceptability of a Novel Prehospital Emergency Care System Evaluation Tool Among Southeast Asian Stakeholders: A Cross-Sectional Survey.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Prehospital emergency care (PEC) systems vary widely in structure, capacity, and stage of development, and existing evaluation tools are not tailored to the contextual needs of Southeast Asia. To address this gap, the Prehospital Emergency Care System Evaluation Tool (PECSET) was developed as a 32-element, consensus-derived framework to support system assessment, prioritization, and quality improvement. The objective of this study was to evaluate the prospective acceptability of the PECSET framework among Southeast Asian prehospital stakeholders using the theoretical framework of acceptability (TFA) and to identify regional variation in implementation priorities.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of PEC professionals from the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, and Malaysia between April 2023 and June 2024. Participants were recruited from six resuscitation training conferences and attended a standardized two-hour educational session before completing an anonymous survey mapped to TFA constructs. We assessed differences between countries using Pearson chi-square tests. Our primary outcome measure was acceptability scores across five TFA domains (affective attitude, intervention coherence, opportunity costs, self-efficacy, and perceived effectiveness). Secondary outcomes included identification of high-priority implementation elements.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Participants (N = 274; 66% response rate) included physicians (46%, n = 126), prehospital professionals (30%, n = 82), and medical directors (15%, n = 41). Intervention coherence was high: 92% to 100% of participants were likely or extremely likely to use PECSET for quality improvement. However, geographic variation existed; a small subset in Indonesia and Vietnam (n = 6) reported they were "unlikely" to use the tool, compared to none in Thailand, Malaysia, and the Philippines (P = .04). Regarding self-efficacy, while 100% (n = 274; 95% CI, 98-100%) reported confidence in application, only 20% (n = 55; 95% CI,15-25%) were "extremely confident." Affective attitude was positive, with 97% (n = 266) intending to integrate the tool; only Vietnam (n = 4; 5% [95% CI, 2-10%]) and Indonesia (n = 2; 2% [95% CI, 0-13%]) indicated hesitation (P = .24). Secondary outcomes identified "layperson public awareness and education programs" as the top implementation priority across all five nations, although priorities varied.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The Prehospital Emergency Care System Evaluation Tool demonstrated high acceptability among potential end-users across Southeast Asia, indicating readiness for broader implementation and future evaluation of feasibility, fidelity, and system-level impact. As a stakeholder-informed evaluation framework, PECSET offers a practical approach to strengthening PEC systems in Southeast Asia and beyond.

articles.title: Recovery of Running and Technical Match Performance After Adductor Muscle Strain Injury in Male Professional Football Players: A Prospective Cohort Study of 27 Players From One LaLiga Team Across Five Seasons.
articles.journal_full: Scandinavian journal of medicine & science in sports

abstract.text: Post return-to-play (RTP) running and technical match performance after adductor muscle strain injury remains unclear. The aim of the present study was to examine recovery of running and technical match performance after RTP following acute adductor muscle strain injury in professional football. This prospective longitudinal cohort study followed players from one team (n = 122) across five seasons (2020/2021-2024/2025). Injuries were recorded by the medical staff and confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging. Match performance variables included playing time, total distance, high-speed running distance (> 24 km/h), number of sprints (> 24 km/h), and offensive and defensive technical actions. First eight matches following RTP were compared with the four pre-injury matches. RTP required unrestricted team training and medical clearance for match selection. Data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations methods, adjusting event counts for the amount of playing time. Of the 122 players, 27 sustained at least one acute adductor muscle strain injury, accounting for 54 injury episodes. At Match 1, time played was -7.1% versus PRE (95% CI -16.7% to +3.5%), total-distance rate -0.4% (-2.4% to +1.5%), high-speed running distance +6.9% (-3.5% to +18.5%), and number of sprints +5.9% (-4.0% to +16.8%); none remained significant after FDR adjustment (p ≥ 0.182; pFDR ≥ 0.817). At Match 8, total passes were 26.5% below PRE (95% CI -50.0% to +7.9%; raw p = 0.116; pFDR = 0.567). Across all Match 1-8 contrasts, only long passes at Match 3 remained significant after FDR adjustment (-15.3%; 95% CI -22.4% to -7.6%; raw p < 0.001; pFDR = 0.022). In conclusion, there was little evidence of systematic population-level impairment in running or technical match performance after RTP. Late passing reductions warrant confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

articles.title: Subclinical Left Ventricular Hypertrophy Among Emergency Department Patients With Elevated Blood Pressure.
articles.journal_full: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hypertension (HTN) is a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, yet early detection of target organ damage is often missed, particularly in patients with limited access to care. The Emergency Department (ED), a key site of care for underserved populations, may offer an opportunity for risk stratification; we sought to determine the prevalence of LVH-a marker of subclinical disease and increased cardiovascular risk-among ED patients with asymptomatic elevated blood pressure and assess differences by sex, race, and insurance status.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We enrolled a convenience sample of adults aged 18-65 years presenting to an academic ED with blood pressure ≥ 140 mmHg systolic or ≥ 90 mmHg diastolic on two measurements. Subjects with prior LVH, active cardiac disease, hypertensive emergency, dialysis dependence, or pregnancy were excluded. LVH was identified using left ventricular mass indexed to height2.7 or body surface area via focused (point-of-care) cardiac ultrasound (parasternal long-axis view). Multivariate logistic regression assessed associations with LVH.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 155 subjects, 46 (29.7%, 95% CI 22.5%-36.9%) had LVH. Mean age was 46.9 ± 12.1 years; 53.6% were women. LVH was more prevalent in women (38.6% vs. 19.4%; p = 0.009) and remained independently associated with female sex (OR 2.44, 95% CI 1.14-5.22, p = 0.021) and prior hypertension (OR 2.47, 95% CI 1.14-5.39, p = 0.023). Notably, 18.3% of patients without a prior hypertension diagnosis demonstrated LVH (p = 0.004).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Nearly one-third of ED patients with elevated blood pressure had LVH, including many without known hypertension, with a higher prevalence among women.

abstract.label: TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05730309.

articles.title: Reduction in Emergency Department Attendances for Acute Bronchiolitis in Infants Aged Under 1 Year in England During Winter 2025/2026 Following Introduction of Maternal RSV Vaccination.

abstract.text: In September 2024, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) maternal vaccination was introduced to the UK schedule. Monitoring acute bronchiolitis emergency department (ED) attendance levels may provide a 'real-world' assessment of the likely impact. ED acute bronchiolitis attendances in England were substantially lower (-23%) in infants aged under 1 year in 2025/2026 compared to preceding seasons, consistent with bronchiolitis aetiology, vaccine efficacy and uptake and RSV immunisation programme impacts elsewhere. This work contributes to the evidence that maternal RSV vaccination is bringing about reductions in the RSV burden in young infants.

articles.title: [Comparison of prehospital management of selected emergencies between a paramedical team and a physician-led team : a retrospective study in Belgium].

abstract.text: In Belgium, the emergency medical system (EMS) coordinates mobile emergency and resuscitation units (SMUR) and paramedical intervention teams (PIT). As demand increases, greater use of PITs could help relieve SMUR workload, although comparative data remain limited. This retrospective study compared prehospital care by analysing 2,325 prehospital interventions (PIT = 1,377; SMUR = 948) involving cardiac arrest, trauma, seizures, chest pain, and acute respiratory disorders. Patient characteristics, response times, and management strategies were analysing. Management of cardiac arrest and seizures was comparable between the two intervention systems. In trauma cases, both patient characteristics and therapeutic interventions differed. In patients with chest pain, SMUR teams performed more electrocardiograms. For respiratory conditions, PIT teams more frequently administered oxygen therapy and aerosol treatment, whereas SMUR teams more often performed intubation. No difference was observed in response times. Overall, PIT appears to be a useful alternative when SMUR is unavailable; however, prospective studies are needed before confirming comparable performance between the two systems.

articles.title: [Gastric volvulus and wandering spleen : a case study].

abstract.text: A 2-year-old child is admitted in the emergency room for abdominal pain and signs of partial intestinal obstruction. Imaging highlights two rare digestive malformations: a gastric volvulus and a wandering spleen. The diagnosis can be challenging due to the non-specific nature of the symptoms in children but should be made early in order to avoid life-threatening complications.

articles.title: Ultrasound and CT Features of Isolated Gallbladder Torsion With a Suspected Congenital Anomaly in a Cat: An Imaging Diagnosis.
articles.journal_full: Veterinary radiology & ultrasound : the official journal of the American College of Veterinary Radiology and the International Veterinary Radiology Association

abstract.text: An 8-month-old domestic short-haired cat was presented to the emergency room with an episode of peracute vomiting and abdominal pain. Ultrasound and computed tomography (CT) examination revealed an abnormally positioned and distended gallbladder with a thickened gallbladder wall. A presumptive diagnosis of gallbladder torsion was made and subsequently confirmed during laparotomy. Although uncommon, gallbladder torsion should be considered a differential diagnosis in feline patients with clinical signs of abdominal pain and peracute vomiting.

articles.title: Validation of ICD-10-CM Codes for Bleeding in Patients With an Indication for Antithrombotic Therapy.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: International Classification of Disease Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes are used to identify adverse drug events. Our goal was to assess accuracy of ICD-10-CM code assignments in billing data for identifying hospital encounters for overt bleeds.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Multicenter, case-control study of patients with indications for antithrombotic therapy and who had an emergency department or hospital admission. Cases identified by ICD-10-CM codes for bleeding were matched 2:1 to controls. Medical record abstraction was the reference standard for determining bleeding occurrence and anatomical location. Diagnostic accuracy of ICD-10-CM codes for bleeding overall was calculated while adjusting for oversampling of cases.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 4803 patients (3140 cases, 1663 controls), ICD-10-CM codes for bleeds in any position had positive predictive value (PPV) of 88.5% (95% CI, 87.4%-89.7%) and adjusted sensitivity of 75.2% (70.9%-79.4%). Intracranial bleed codes had the highest PPV (93.1%; 95% CI, 91.3%-94.9%) and adjusted sensitivity (100%; 95% CI, 94.0%-100.0%). Gastrointestinal bleed codes and codes for other bleeds had PPVs (95% CI) of 83.1% (81.2%-85.0%) and 77.2% (74.6%-79.8%) and adjusted sensitivities (95% CI) of 84.8% (78.5%-91.1%) and 52.2% (46.2%-58.8%), respectively. Restricting codes to the primary diagnosis position increased PPV of any bleed to 97.2% (96.5%-97.9%), but decreased adjusted sensitivity to 44.9% (40.79%-49.6%). Codes for antithrombotic poisoning/adverse effect had PPV of 88.4% (83.9%-93.0%) but adjusted sensitivity of 5.6% (5.3%-5.9%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: When using ICD-10-CM codes to identify overt bleeding in patients who have an indication for antithrombotic therapy, codes in the primary position have the highest PPV. Use of codes in any position maximizes sensitivity.

articles.title: Spontaneous Posture at Emergency Department Arrival as a Behavioral Signal of Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Prospective Study.
articles.journal_full: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To determine whether spontaneous body posture at emergency department arrival is associated with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and whether its addition improves apparent model discrimination beyond established clinical risk scores.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a prospective, single-center observational study using convenience sampling during investigators' 24-h clinical shifts, including nights and weekends. Adults undergoing evaluation for possible ACS were eligible. Spontaneous posture was recorded on an ED stretcher within 1-2 min of arrival or transfer, before clinician-directed positioning, using six categories. Cardiologists blinded to posture adjudicated ACS. Firth regression adjusted for age, sex, and coronary artery disease. Sensitivity analyses accounted for arrival mode and excluded ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). HEART and TIMI discrimination analyses excluded STEMI and used bootstrap correction for optimism.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 225 participants, 64 (28.4%) had ACS: 12 STEMIs, 48 non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarctions, and four cases of unstable angina. Compared with leaning back, tripod/forward-leaning posture (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 7.54; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.46-25.48) and arm-supported posture (aOR, 6.91; 95% CI, 1.83-29.16) were associated with higher ACS odds. The global posture association persisted after arrival-mode adjustment and STEMI exclusion. In the separate 30-patient reliability sample, unweighted Cohen's κ was 0.945 (95% CI, 0.725-1.000). Among 213 patients without STEMI, adding posture increased the optimism-corrected area under the curve from 0.8709 to 0.8950 for HEART and from 0.8208 to 0.8800 for TIMI.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Spontaneous posture was associated with ACS in this cohort, including after STEMI exclusion. Posture provided incremental discrimination beyond HEART and TIMI, but ACS specificity and clinical decision benefit remain unestablished. External validation is required before clinical use.

articles.title: Measles resurgence in England: challenges in maintaining elimination, 2023 to 2024.
articles.journal_full: Euro surveillance : bulletin Europeen sur les maladies transmissibles = European communicable disease bulletin

abstract.text: BACKGROUNDBetween October 2023 and September 2024, England experienced the largest measles outbreak in decades.AIMWe describe the epidemiology of the outbreak, burden on secondary care services and the factors that led to this resurgence.METHODSThe UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) conducts enhanced surveillance of all suspected measles cases in England. A measles line list was established using routinely collected notification, laboratory, demographic and vaccination information. Laboratory-confirmed cases were defined using serology and PCR. Incidence rates were calculated using mid-2024 population estimates. Severity was assessed through linkage with emergency department attendances, hospital admissions and length of stay.RESULTSMost of the 2,821 laboratory-confirmed cases resided in London (n = 1,283; 45.5%) and in the West Midlands (n = 710; 25.2%). Incidence was highest in London (14.1/100,000 population). Children under 10 years represented 58.6% (n = 1,653) of cases. Most cases (n = 2,609; 92.5%) were not vaccinated, and 63.0% (n = 1,776) lived in areas belonging to the two most deprived quintiles. Of the 2,788 cases that could be linked to hospitalisation data, 76.3% (n = 2,127) attended emergency care and 38.2% (n = 1,066) were admitted. Median length of stay was 2.0 days, seven cases received intensive care; one death was reported. Admissions were highest among infants aged < 1 year (51.6%, 165/320) and adults ≥ 30 years (47.2%, 195/413).CONCLUSIONThis outbreak reflects a shift towards endemic measles transmission in areas of high deprivation and low vaccine uptake in England. It underscores the importance of achieving 95% uptake with measles vaccine in all areas and communities to achieve and maintain elimination.

articles.title: Intervention-driven reduction in potentially inappropriate medication use amongst older adults in long-term care facilities in South Korea.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
