abstract.text: Polypharmacy and potentially inappropriate medication (PIM) use are common in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) and are associated with adverse outcomes; evidence from Asian settings is limited.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate the effect of a multidisciplinary medication management programme on medication and PIM use and on serious adverse events (SAEs).

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Cluster randomised controlled trial in 28 LTCFs (16 intervention, 12 control).

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: LTCFs in the Seoul metropolitan area, South Korea.

abstract.label: SUBJECTS
abstract.text: 1672 residents aged ≥65 years (836 per group).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Intervention facilities delivered comprehensive medication review, deprescribing recommendations and multidisciplinary case conferences; control facilities provided usual care. Assessments were made at baseline and at 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 months. The number of PIMs and PIM user status were the primary outcomes; SAEs (falls, emergency department [ED] visits and hospitalisations) were pre-specified but not powered for. Medication outcomes were analysed with generalised linear mixed models and SAEs with Fine-Grey competing-risk models, both accounting for facility-level clustering and adjusted for 10 baseline covariates.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Over 15 months, medication and PIM counts increased in the control but not the intervention group (time-by-group incidence rate ratio 0.993, 95% CI 0.990-0.996, P < .001, and .990, 0.983-0.997, P = .004). PIM users fell from 65.8% to 62.5% in the intervention arm and rose from 72.5% to 75.5% in the control arm (OR 0.981, 0.962-0.999, P = .043; not significant in the per-protocol analysis). ED visits or hospitalisations were less frequent in the intervention arm (27.6% vs 32.3%) but the difference was not significant (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.740, 0.493-1.112, P = .147); falls did not differ (P = .762).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: A multidisciplinary medication management programme was associated with reduced medication and PIM use. ED visits and hospitalisations were less frequent in the intervention arm, but not significantly so after accounting for facility-level clustering; the trial was not powered for these events and confirmation is needed.

articles.title: Within-season recurrent sport-related concussions prolong return-to-play timeline in professional collision sport athletes.
articles.journal_full: Journal of science and medicine in sport

abstract.text: Return-to-play (RTPg) timelines were examined in professional Australian rules football and rugby league athletes following sport-related concussion (SRCh) during the 2024 season. Among 24 SRC cases, no significant differences in RTP duration were found between athletes with or without prior SRC history. However, a second SRC within the same season was associated with a substantially longer RTP duration. These findings highlight the importance of cautious, individualised RTP decision-making following repeat concussions, particularly in contact and collision sports.

articles.title: Bilateral renal infarction unmasking rheumatic mitral valve disease with left atrial appendage thrombus in sinus rhythm: a case report.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Acute renal infarction mimics pyelonephritis and is frequently missed at first presentation. Rheumatic mitral stenosis can cause systemic embolism even in sinus rhythm.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 47-year-old Thai man presented with four days of evolving abdominal pain, previously attributed to gastroenteritis and treated symptomatically at a first emergency visit. He had fever without chills, left costovertebral-angle tenderness, and a bland urinalysis. Point-of-care ultrasound was atypical for pyelonephritis; computed tomography showed bilateral wedge-shaped cortical defects with a cortical rim sign but could not exclude focal bacterial nephritis. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound demonstrated an avascular left upper pole, confirming bland infarction, supported by lactate dehydrogenase 1194 U/L, procalcitonin 0.28 ng/mL, and sterile cultures. Echocardiography revealed rheumatic mitral valve disease with clinically significant stenosis (valve area 1.34 cm2 by planimetry; diastolic doming, commissural fusion, fish-mouth orifice) and moderate regurgitation. The left atrium was dilated, with dense spontaneous echo contrast and a left atrial appendage thrombus despite sinus rhythm. Enoxaparin with overlapping warfarin was started; a direct oral anticoagulant was avoided. At 2 months the patient was in New York Heart Association class II without recurrent embolism, but the international normalized ratio had not yet reached target; repeat transoesophageal echocardiography is scheduled at 3 months.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound can resolve the computed tomography ambiguity between infarction and focal bacterial nephritis at the bedside. In mitral stenosis, a prior embolic event or left atrial thrombus mandates vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation irrespective of rhythm, and an appendage thrombus and coexisting mitral regurgitation defer balloon commissurotomy.

articles.title: On-Scene Time-Dependent Probabilities of Return of Spontaneous Circulation and Favorable Neurological Outcome in Cases of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with an Initial Shockable Rhythm: A Retrospective Study Using the National Utstein Data in Japan.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with an initial shockable rhythm, the likelihood of achieving on-scene return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and favorable neurological outcomes changes with elapsed resuscitation time. We aimed to describe these time-dependent patterns under existing Japanese emergency medical services (EMS) practice. Methods: We conducted a nationwide retrospective descriptive cohort study using linked Japanese Utstein and emergency transport data from 2017-2022. Adults with cardiogenic OHCA and an initial shockable rhythm were included. For each time point after EMS contact, we calculated the observed probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC and, among patients achieving on-scene ROSC, the probability of a favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2 at 1 month) according to ROSC timing. Results: Among 22,383 eligible patients, 5095 achieved on-scene ROSC and 3182 had favorable neurological outcomes. The probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC was 6.97% (1295/18,583; 95% CI, 6.61-7.34%) at 10 min and 0.50% (87/17,375; 95% CI, 0.41-0.62%) at 20 min. At 10 min, favorable neurological outcomes occurred in 50.0% of patients aged <75 years and 20.5% of those aged ≥75 years who achieved on-scene ROSC at or after that time point. A sensitivity analysis restricted to 3128 patients receiving first EMS defibrillation within 1 min showed broadly similar temporal patterns. Conclusions: Under existing Japanese EMS practice, subsequent on-scene ROSC and favorable neurological outcomes became less frequent with later ROSC timing. Younger patients showed more favorable neurological outcomes at later ROSC times, but these findings do not establish age-based criteria for prolonged resuscitation or transport decisions.

articles.title: Vegetarian dietary patterns are not associated with lower odds of noncommunicable diseases among patients presenting to a tertiary care center in North India: a cross-sectional survey.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) present a huge global burden, accounting for approximately 7.3 trillion cases and 43.8 million deaths in 2021. In India, 68% of all deaths are caused by NCDs. Carbohydrate intake has been associated with NCD development. Standard Indian diets mainly comprise carbohydrates. In this study, we aimed to analyze the association of vegetarian versus omnivorous diets with the odds of developing NCDs in patients visiting the emergency department.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Over 18 months, a cross-sectional epidemiological survey-based study was conducted among patients aged >18 years presenting to our department with documented comorbid conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus [DM], hypertension, heart disease, hypothyroidism, Alzheimer disease, and cancer). These patients completed a 32-item questionnaire survey regarding dietary and lifestyle choices. Associations between comorbidity status and dietary variables were evaluated by bivariate analysis. Additionally, unadjusted odds ratio (OR) and adjusted OR for DM, hypertension, and heart disease were calculated.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: This study included 11,011 patients, of which 55.31% were males and 68.91% were >55 years old. Furthermore, 65.87% were vegetarians, whereas 28.97% were omnivores. Hypertension, DM, and heart disease were found in 62.6%, 49.9% and 26.0%, respectively, while 58% had combinations of NCDs. Adjusted for age, sex, smoking, sugar, alcohol, exercise, and packaged food, OR (omnivore vs. vegetarian) was 0.94 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.86-1.03; P=0.180), 0.91 (95% CI, 0.83-1.00; P=0.052) and 1.02 (95% CI, 0.92-1.13; P=0.690) for DM, hypertension, and heart disease, respectively.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Most patients with NCDs followed a vegetarian dietary pattern, which was not associated with lower odds of developing NCDs.

articles.title: Built environment and emergency medical services response time in a high-density megacity: multilevel evidence from urban-suburban.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency medical services (EMS) response time is a key indicator for evaluating the performance of public health system and is closely associated with patient survival rates. However, empirical evidence on the potential relationship between the built environment and EMS response time remains limited, restricting the development of spatially informed strategies for improving EMS system operations.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This study employed 2024 ambulance dispatch data from the Beijing Emergency Center Office Management System, combined with multi-source data on the built environment, to construct a multilevel regression model examining the influence of subdistrict (township)-level built environment factors on EMS response time and investigating the heterogeneity between urban areas and suburbs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The results indicate that, at the citywide level, lower residential facility density and denser arterial and local road networks significantly reduced EMS response time. Specifically, while in central urban areas, high densities of residential facilities were associated with longer response time, in suburban areas, higher densities of local roads enhanced EMS efficiency.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: These findings provide valuable evidence to guide built environment interventions aimed at shortening EMS response time and improving service efficiency across different areas.

articles.title: Spatial optimization of vaccine supply networks in complex terrains: balancing economic feasibility and public health equity.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Vaccine supply planning in hazard-prone terrains faces compounding geographic, socioeconomic, and operational barriers. Conventional models relying on planar distances and static metrics often fail to capture true accessibility disparities, often driving inefficient infrastructure allocation and exacerbating health inequities.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: This study develops an integrated decision-making framework coupling spatial equity, economic feasibility, and multi-scenario resilience to systematically reconfigure the vaccine supply network across 183 counties in Sichuan, China.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Using high-resolution road network data from the AMap Application Programming Interface (API), we model actual geographic impedance based on travel time. An adapted two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) method, embedded with socioeconomic vulnerability indicators, pinpoints baseline accessibility disparities. Candidate hubs are selected via entropy-weighted Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) combined with spatial-equity quotas, and a candidate-pool capacity-sufficiency check (α coefficient) determines the final candidate-pool size. A multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming (MO-MILP) model then co-optimizes hub configuration, capacity scaling, and cross-regional dispatch, endogenously balancing operational efficiency, equity penalties, and capacity expansion costs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Under entropy-weighted TOPSIS ranking with spatial-equity quotas, the initial 61-hub pool (including 21 existing CDC anchors) provides aggregate capacity equal to 82% of total demand. The capacity-sufficiency rule therefore expands the pool to C* = 103 hubs that satisfy Cap(C*) ≥ 1.2 × total demand. The optimized baseline network (103 candidate hubs, 99 with positive flows) achieves zero unmet demand through endogenous capacity expansion and single-source assignment, with a total objective value of 18,510,357. Sensitivity analysis across α = 1.0-1.4 shows that higher sufficiency coefficients increase the candidate pool (76 → 150 hubs) while reducing required capacity expansion by 63%. Fixed-topology resilience tests indicate zero shortages under all structural failure scenarios when emergency expansion is permitted, whereas zero-expansion stress tests bound shortage-free surge tolerance between +10% and +20% demand growth.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Integrating spatial equity and capacity sufficiency at the candidate-pool stage limits the risk that pool-level capacity deficits are later compensated through node-level expansion. The α coefficient serves as a planning parameter for balancing network redundancy and expansion needs. The α = 1.2 configuration provides a robust and equitable vaccine supply network for mountainous regions under the model's cost assumptions.

articles.title: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest as the First Manifestation of ALCAPA in a 9-Week-Old Infant: Survival to Discharge After Emergency Repair and VA-ECMO.

abstract.text: Background and Clinical Significance: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) usually presents with heart failure at 2-3 months of age; cardiac arrest as the first manifestation is rare and often recognized only at autopsy. Case Presentation: A previously healthy girl collapsed at home at 65 days of age. After dispatcher-assisted parental resuscitation, the emergency team found asystole and achieved return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 4 min of professional resuscitation; the total low-flow time was not recorded. She was in cardiogenic shock (left ventricular ejection fraction 19.8%, high-sensitivity troponin T 2620 ng/L) with acute kidney injury and coagulopathy consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation. Echocardiography showed a dilated right coronary artery and no flow from the aorta into the left coronary artery. Emergency repair on day 1 was followed by venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) for 4 days and continuous renal replacement therapy. The Simpson ejection fraction reached about 50% by day 9, fell to 37-40% during respiratory deterioration and was 45-50% on day 27; mitral regurgitation, graded as massive during VA-ECMO, regressed to trace without valve surgery. She was discharged on day 42 with impaired diastolic indices; no formal neurological assessment was documented. Conclusions: ALCAPA should be considered in every infant with unexplained cardiac arrest, and post-resuscitation echocardiography should assess the coronary origins. Emergency repair with VA-ECMO can achieve survival to discharge despite multiorgan failure, but long-term cardiac and neurodevelopmental follow-up is required.

articles.title: Vascular and Extremity Injuries in Disasters.
articles.journal_full: The Surgical clinics of North America

abstract.text: Disasters and mass casualty incidents generate extremity and vascular injury patterns distinct from routine civilian trauma. Blast injuries produce extremity vascular injury rates of 8.6% to 10%, earthquakes generate crush syndrome in up to 25% of victims with lower extremity involvement in 74% to 82% of cases, and mass shootings demonstrate vascular injury rates of 8% to 29%. This review examines the unique mechanisms and epidemiology of extremity injuries in these disaster scenarios and provides evidence-based management strategies including tourniquet application, temporary vascular shunts, damage control orthopedics, fasciotomy timing, and amputation decision-making.

articles.title: Sex differences in bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation and survival to hospital discharge for public out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in North Carolina and Singapore: a retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: Women are less likely to receive bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in public. The study aims to assess if sex in patients with public out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCAs), was associated with bystander CPR and survival to hospital discharge, in North Carolina and Singapore.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult (≥18 years) OHCAs of the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (North Carolina, 2013-2022) and the Pan-Asian Resuscitation Outcomes Study (Singapore, 2010-2020). Using multivariable logistic regression, we examined the association of sex with bystander CPR and survival to hospital discharge adjusting for potential confounding variables (e.g. age, year of arrest).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We analyzed data from 6828 OHCAs in North Carolina and 3617 OHCAs in Singapore. Public bystander CPR rates were 48% for males and 44% for females in North Carolina [adjusted odd ratio (aOR) 0.87; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.77, 0.99], and 59% for males and 52% for females in Singapore [aOR 0.78; 95% CI (0.62, 0.98)]. The proportion surviving to hospital discharge in North Carolina were 24% for males and 26% for females [aOR 1.15; 95% CI (1.00, 1.33)], and 12% for males and 9% for females in Singapore [aOR 0.63; 95% CI (0.43, 0.93)].

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Females were less likely to receive bystander CPR than males in public in both North Carolina and Singapore, irrespective of age. However, females were less likely to survive to hospital discharge compared to males in Singapore, whereas the opposite was seen in North Carolina.

articles.title: Initial shockable rhythm detection among patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest by arrest location: A population-based cohort study in Japan.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: We described the patient characteristics, bystander interventions, and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) according to arrest location, focusing on initial rhythm and automated external defibrillator (AED) use.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We analyzed medical-origin OHCAs from a population-based registry (2016-2024) by arrest location: home, nursing home, or other locations. Patient characteristics, bystander interventions, and outcomes were summarized descriptively. Multivariable logistic regression examined the association between arrest location and initial shockable rhythm.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 2478 OHCA cases, initial shockable rhythm was identified in 36.3% (221/609) in nursing homes, 7.1% (113/1582) at home, and 33.4% (96/287) in other locations. After adjustment, the odds of an initial shockable rhythm were higher in nursing homes than at home (adjusted OR, 12.35; 95% CI, 8.93-17.24) and than in other locations (adjusted OR, 2.35; 95% CI, 1.60-3.45). In nursing homes, 96.8% (214/221) of patients with an initial shockable rhythm received an AED shock. One-month survival with favorable neurological outcomes was the lowest in nursing homes (0.8% [5/609]).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Initial shockable rhythm was identified in more than one-third of arrests occurring in nursing homes, and 97% of these patients received an AED shock. This finding may partly reflect earlier AED access, potentially increasing the likelihood of detecting a shockable rhythm soon after collapse. These findings underscore the importance of early rhythm detection through prompt AED use and suggest that extending AED access to home settings warrants further investigation.

articles.title: Experiences and coping strategies of bystanders involved in out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a qualitative study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Participating in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can have a substantial emotional and psychological impact on bystanders. Understanding their experiences and coping strategies may inform supportive interventions that could mitigate the impact on future bystanders.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The study used a qualitative research design grounded in an experiential orientation. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with people who had been involved in CPR during an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in Scotland outside of a professional role. Participants were recruited via social media advertisements. We transcribed and analysed interviews using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eleven interviews were conducted between November 2024 and April 2025. Most bystanders knew the person (n = 9, 81%) as a family member, team member or neighbour. Most were female (n = 9, 82%) and were non-healthcare professionals (n = 7, 64%). Seven of those who experienced OHCA survived, three died, and one outcome was unknown. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four interconnected themes: Emotional impact; Managing multiple roles and responsibilities; Compelled to help but unprepared; and Talking to the right person.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Findings from the interviews with bystanders suggest that OHCA can have a substantial emotional impact, particularly when the person dies or is known to the bystander. Several ways to reduce this impact were identified, including greater emotional preparation in CPR training, involvement in activities that prepare themselves or others for OHCA/CPR, and opportunities to speak with an independent person knowledgeable about OHCA/CPR. Future research should investigate the effectiveness of incorporating these strategies into support interventions for OHCA bystanders.

articles.title: Prehospital Detection of Acute Pulmonary Embolism and Its Association with Clinical Outcomes: A Retrospective Cohort Study.

abstract.text: Background: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potentially life-threatening condition requiring timely diagnosis and treatment. However, data on prehospital correct PE detection by emergency medical services (EMS) are scarce. Methods: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study at the BG University Hospital Bergmannsheil Bochum, Germany, including all patients with in-hospital confirmed PE (ICD-10: I26.0/I26.9) and admitted by EMS between January 2019 and December 2024. Prehospital PE detection was defined as documentation of PE as the working diagnosis in the EMS protocol. Time to definitive diagnosis was calculated from EMS alarm to computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) acquisition. Multivariable Cox regression and logistic and linear regression models were used to identify predictors of time to diagnosis and clinical outcomes. Main Results: Of 171 patients included, prehospital PE was correctly suspected in only nine cases (5.3%, 95% CI 2.8-9.7%). Time to definitive diagnosis was significantly shorter in patients with correct prehospital PE recognition than in those without (median 2.1 vs. 4.0 h, log-rank p < 0.001). In an exploratory analysis, detection occurred only in physician-staffed EMS encounters (10.8% vs. 0%, p = 0.003). Prehospital intravenous heparin, administered predominantly for suspected myocardial infarction, was also associated with a higher rate of CTPA acquisition, 2.42 (95% CI 1.40-4.19), likely reflecting confounding by indication. Overall, 56 patients (33.1%) were not diagnosed within 6 h of emergency department presentation; 38 (22.5%) were diagnosed only after more than 24 h. Conclusions: Correct detection of PE by EMS is critically low, yet correct detection is associated with earlier imaging. These findings highlight the urgent need for EMS-specific diagnostic strategies and prospective trials to improve prehospital PE detection.

articles.title: Surface Temperature Control After Cardiac Arrest in the Emergency Department Without Feedback-Controlled Devices: An Observational Single-Centre Cohort Study of Routine Care.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Guidelines recommend active fever prevention after cardiac arrest, yet many emergency departments (EDs) lack feedback-controlled temperature-management devices. We describe what simple surface methods achieved in one ED. Methods: Observational cohort of 123 comatose adults with return of spontaneous circulation treated with routine care in a university ED (2017-2020; records to March 2019 analysed retrospectively, later documentation collected prospectively). Technique and length of the management period (12 h or 24 h) were chosen by the treating physician without a written protocol: ice packs (n = 51), ice packs plus a forced-air blanket at its lowest heated setting (32 °C; n = 45), a thin sheet only (n = 21), forced air alone (n = 4) or a circulating-water device (n = 2). Trajectories were compared in a mixed-effects model; the primary endpoint, revised post hoc from the original target of ≤36.0 °C, was fever (≥37.7 °C) after cessation. Results: Ice packs plus forced air gave lower temperatures than ice packs alone from 4 h (adjusted difference -0.68 °C, 95% CI -0.95 to -0.41) to 24 h (-0.44 °C), but overshot below 35.0 °C more often (34/45 vs. 9/51). Fever after cessation was more frequent after physician-selected 12 h than 24 h periods (23/33 vs. 6/90) and in the thin-sheet group (20/21). All 21 thin-sheet patients died; baseline differences suggest allocation by prognosis, and mortality was not analysed causally. Conclusions: Ice packs with or without forced air kept most patients below the fever threshold for up to 36 h; the combination cooled more, which did not mean better control. Safety could not be assessed, and randomised evaluation is needed.

articles.title: Semi-Supervised 2D Pose Estimation for Underwater Divers via Limb-Heatmap-Guided Bidirectional Cross-Representation Consistency Learning.

abstract.text: Underwater image degradation and occlusion make diver keypoints less visually discernible, leading to substantial localization errors in the keypoint pseudo-labels generated by existing semi-supervised methods. These errors can then accumulate and propagate during consistency learning. Moreover, these methods do not fully exploit the human structural information available in unlabeled images. To address these limitations, a limb-heatmap-guided bidirectional cross-representation consistency method is proposed for semi-supervised learning. A keypoint network and a limb network are employed to learn point-level keypoint responses and region-level limb-structure responses, respectively. For labeled data, limb labels are generated automatically from keypoint annotations and a predefined skeletal topology, without additional annotations. For unlabeled data, intra-representation consistency learning is performed for both networks between the easy-augmentation and hard-augmentation views, and bidirectional cross-representation supervision is applied between the two networks. In the keypoint-to-limb path, keypoint predictions are converted into limb pseudo-labels to supervise the limb network; in the limb-to-keypoint path, limb heatmaps reconstructed from keypoint predictions are compared with the predictions of the limb network to constrain the keypoint configuration. During model inference, only the keypoint network is retained, with no additional inference cost. On the independent test set of a single underwater diver dataset constructed for this study, the proposed method achieves a mean PCKh@0.5 of 80.07% using all labeled training data and outperforms the comparison methods at labeled-data proportions of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. These results demonstrate that region-level limb structure provides effective complementary supervision for point-level keypoint localization within the evaluated setting. Broader applicability requires further validation.

articles.title: Prehospital Facial Recognition Technology: Randomized Controlled Simulation Study.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The risk of medical errors increases for the approximately 689,000 unidentified, noncommunicative patients who present to emergency departments annually. The concomitant rise in hospital admissions, lengths of stay, and mortality will likely persist unless approaches to identifying noncommunicative patients are developed and adopted. Facial recognition technology could provide a solution where scanning the face reliably provides access to identification and medical history of patients who self-enroll in the application database. Our objective was to compare paramedics' ability to identify noncommunicative patients and make related clinical decisions using a cloud-based facial-recognition application vs standard practice.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a double-blind, randomized controlled study with 90 participating firefighterparamedics in a simulated patient encounter. Our primary outcome was patient identification. Secondary outcomes included identification of key medical information, appropriateness of treatment decisions, and transport to the patient's preferred hospital. We uploaded facial photographs and simulated medical profiles to a secure cloud-based app. Participants used a tablet to scan the patient's face (standardized patient or actor). Successful matches returned identifying information, medical history, emergency contacts, preferred hospital, and primary care physician contact information. The 48 experimental participants had access to this patient information, while the 42 controls did not, even if they scanned the face. Standardized patients (SP) portrayed a noncommunicative urosepsis patient. Participants reported their findings to the facilitators and evaluated the technology on a 5-point Likert scale.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We analyzed 90 study participants (48 experimental, 42 control), of whom 40/48 (83.3%) experimental group identified the SP compared with 9/42 (21.4%) control group (OR [odds ratio], 13.87; 95% CI, 5.03-38.25; P < .001). Identification of important medical information of the SP by the study participants occurred in 30/48 (62.5%) in the experimental group versus 4/42 (9.5%) in control (OR, 15.83; 95% CI, 4.84-51.76; P < .001). Correct transport decision to the preferred hospital occurred in 27/48 (56.3%) experimental participants compared with 10/42 (23.8%) controls (OR, 4.11; 95% CI, 1.65-10.23; P = .02). Overall, 80% of participants reported that the technology would benefit their day-to-day clinical work.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The use of a cloud-based facial-recognition application significantly improved firefighter-paramedics' ability to identify noncommunicative patients and access critical medical information, with an appropriate transport decision to the patient's preferred hospital.

articles.title: Perspectives on Influenza Vaccination Among COVID-19 Unvaccinated Patients in US Emergency Departments: A Qualitative Study.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Efforts to increase influenza vaccine acceptance must consider the importance of patient education and familiarity with vaccinations and influenza in the emergency department (ED), particularly for populations without another primary source of healthcare. This is the first study, to our knowledge, to assess in-depth perceptions regarding the influenza vaccine and identify barriers and facilitators to influenza vaccination among COVID-19 unvaccinated adult ED patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a qualitative idiographic interview study from July 12, 2021, to September 24, 2021, at four EDs in urban cities across the United States. We recruited adult ED patients (18 years and older) unvaccinated for COVID-19, without a primary care clinician, who were fluent in either English or Spanish. The primary finding was a detailed understanding of patient perceptions regarding the influenza vaccine, with secondary findings assessing influenza vaccination rates, barriers and facilitators to being vaccinated, sources of information, and future vaccination intentions. We used a content analysis approach to identify themes around patient experiences, concerns, barriers, information sources, and future intentions regarding influenza vaccination.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 65 participants interviewed, 48 discussed the influenza vaccine and were included in this analysis. Among these participants, the median age was 34 years, 21 (43.8%) were women, and 14 (29.2%) were Hispanic. We found three core themes influencing influenza vaccine hesitancy: 1) previous experiences with influenza illness and/or the vaccine; 2) knowledge about the influenza vaccine; and 3) confidence in vaccine safety and effectiveness. In our cohort, 10 (20.8%) participants demonstrated knowledge of the purpose and mechanism of the influenza vaccine. In addition, 14 (29.2%) patients suggested they would accept the vaccine if offered, while 18 (37.5%) patients stated they did not plan to receive the influenza vaccine and/or expressed strong hesitancy due to concerns about lack of vaccine effectiveness, fear of side effects, and lack of concern regarding influenza illness.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Our findings identify an important barrier that could be overcome by ED-based vaccine education, particularly for underserved patient populations. Interventions to increase influenza vaccine uptake could focus on overcoming hesitancy related to prior experiences and understanding of vaccine safety and effectiveness.

articles.title: Modern management of third nerve palsy: neuroimaging triage and surgical rehabilitation.

abstract.text: Third nerve palsy (TNP) is a complex neuro-ophthalmic condition that requires rapid differentiation between benign microvascular ischemia and life-threatening or otherwise serious causes, including aneurysmal, neoplastic, inflammatory, infectious, demyelinating, traumatic, and cavernous sinus pathologies. Given the high prevalence of diabetes, understanding both pupil-involving and pupil-sparing presentations is critical. Current literature often fragments TNP management across isolated medical specialties. Rather than presenting an evidence-based consensus guideline, this paper provides an expert narrative synthesis proposing a bipartite clinical framework. This framework sequences acute neuro-ophthalmic triage (Weeks 1-12) and chronic ophthalmic rehabilitation (>6 months) to coordinate immediate etiological workup with subsequent surgical and rehabilitative planning. TNP manifestations vary based on the dual anatomy of the third nerve. Compressive lesions typically paralyze superficial pupillomotor fibers, whereas ischemic insults preserve them. Because pupillary status alone cannot definitively rule out emergencies, acute care triage requires neuroimaging tailored to the clinical context. Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) and Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) serve as primary modalities when an aneurysm is suspected; contrast-enhanced MRI is preferred when brainstem, cavernous sinus, orbital, inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic pathology is suspected; and CT is used first in acute trauma. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) is reserved for specific cases to detect microaneurysms smaller than 3 mm when initial imaging is inconclusive. Chronic or unresolving cases are managed through sequentially planned interventions, where strabismus alignment is typically prioritized before ptosis repair. Ultimately, this review proposes an evidence-informed, phase-based framework designed to support the timely identification of potentially fatal etiologies and guide individualized functional and esthetic rehabilitation. Multidisciplinary collaboration, utilizing prospective registries, is essential to address current data gaps and enhance long-term rehabilitative success in patients with TNP.

articles.title: Immediate changes in self-reported apprehension and uncertainty across 41 emergency scenarios following a structured emergency medicine course.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency physicians face high cognitive and emotional stress in acute care, especially in prehospital settings. Structured training is an essential component of emergency medicine education and may increase familiarity with high-pressure clinical situations. In Germany, an 80-hour standardized emergency physician course is mandatory for certification.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE/DESIGN
abstract.text: This study evaluated the impact of this course on physicians' self-perceived apprehension and uncertainty in acute emergency scenarios using a prospective pre-post design.

abstract.label: SETTINGS AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: The study was conducted in five consecutive emergency courses. 162 physicians from different specializations and departments throughout Germany completed pre- and post-course questionnaires.

abstract.label: INTERVENTION
abstract.text: Participants completed the standardized 80 h course, which combines theoretical instruction, structured decision-making, team communication, and high-fidelity simulation.

abstract.label: ANALYSIS
abstract.text: The primary endpoint was the change in a single combined self-reported rating of apprehension and uncertainty, assessed using a 5-point Likert scale across 41 questionnaire items. Analyses of the predefined categories constituted secondary analyses, while analyses of the 41 individual items and subgroup analyses were exploratory.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A significant overall reduction in combined self-reported apprehension and uncertainty was observed. Improvements occurred across all seven predefined categories. The greatest reductions were found for intraosseous access and ocular emergencies. Pediatric and neonatal emergencies remained the most apprehension-provoking scenarios. Exploratory subgroup analyses provided no evidence of differences in improvement across medical specialties or according to board certification status, whereas participants with prior EMS experience showed a smaller improvement than those without prior EMS experience.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Course participation was associated with lower immediate post-course self-reported apprehension/uncertainty scores.

articles.title: Ethics in Disaster Management.
articles.journal_full: The Surgical clinics of North America

abstract.text: In disaster medicine, the traditional pillars of bioethics, namely beneficence, nonmaleficence, autonomy, and justice can be strained. As medical resources are exhausted, providers often pivot from individual-focused care toward a utilitarian framework aimed at maximizing collective survival. This shift introduces complex challenges, including the moral burden of triage, the duty of providers to remain at their posts despite personal risk, and the necessity of grappling with socioeconomic inequities. Ultimately, an effective ethical disaster response requires protocols that preserve the humanity of both patients and providers while functioning within operational realities.

articles.title: Impact of an electronic health record visual cue on time to analgesia in patients with sickle cell in vaso-occlusive crisis.
articles.journal_full: The American journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Management of painful vaso-occlusive crises (VOC), a hallmark of sickle cell disease (SCD), is a critical responsibility of emergency physicians (EPs). However, timely administration of opioid analgesia remains below the American Society of Hematology (ASH) 2020 guideline target.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Our team implemented a technology-based intervention using a salmon-colored visual signal in the Electronic Health Record (EHR) to easily identify ED patients with SCD and prompt clinicians to prioritize patients with VOC. The study examined whether the intervention improved time to opioid administration for SCD VOC in a large urban academic ED.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective pre-post intervention study used EHR data for adult ED encounters with a diagnosis of SCD VOC over one year. The primary predictor was pre-intervention and post-intervention visits. Mixed-effects models examined associations between clinical outcomes and the primary predictor while accounting for repeated visits for VOC by the same patient. The primary outcome was mean time from ED arrival to first opioid administration. Secondary outcome was whether patients received the opioid within 60 min of ED arrival. A sensitivity analysis excluded high ED utilizers at various thresholds; more than 5, 10, 24, and 29 ED visits for SCD VOC.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 841 ED encounters from 168 patients, mean time to first opioid was 66.3 min pre-intervention and 71.7 min post-intervention. Adjusted models indicated that time to first opioid administration was 2.50 min longer post-intervention (95% CI: -4.16 to 9.15). The odds of receiving first opioids within 60 min did not differ between intervention periods (aOR = 0.97, 95% CI: 0.71 to 1.32, absolute difference = 1.7, 95% CI: -5.1 to 8.4). Sensitivity analyses excluding high ED utilizers at four thresholds showed consistent results with primary analysis: 5-visit threshold (247 visits, adjusted difference = 3.4 min, 95% CI: -16.1 to 23); 10-visit threshold (377 visits, adjusted difference = 1.2 min, 95% CI: -11.6 to 14); 24-visit threshold (514 visits, adjusted difference = 4 min, 95% CI: -7.0 to 15.1); 29-visit threshold (572 visits, adjusted difference = 3.5 min, 95% CI: -6.4 to 13.3). None of these results reached statistical significance.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: These findings suggest that passive EHR visual signals alone are insufficient to reduce analgesia delays in VOC, and that meaningful improvement will likely require multi-component, systems-based interventions integrating workflow redesign, nurse-initiated protocols, and automated clinical decision support.

articles.title: Teaching Modalities for Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy Education: A Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To systematically identify and synthesise the available evidence on teaching modalities for hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) education across all learner levels.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, SinoMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library from inception to 15 June 2026 for studies evaluating any HBOT teaching or training intervention against traditional instruction or another comparator, with knowledge, skills, or learner satisfaction as outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for randomised trials, ROBINS-I for comparative non-randomised studies, and MMAT/JBI checklists for descriptive and survey designs. Because of marked design heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively following the SWiM guideline. An exploratory synthesis of extractable effect sizes was undertaken to characterise the direction and magnitude of reported effects. The protocol was retrospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261462169).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Thirty studies met the inclusion criteria (nine English-language, 21 Chinese-language). The evidence base was dominated by single-group pre-post evaluations, descriptive curriculum reports, and cross-sectional surveys; only four randomised controlled trials were identified. Technology-enhanced modalities-simulation-based education, blended/online learning, and Web-based simulation-were generally associated with promising improvements in knowledge and skills, although most studies lacked an active comparator. The exploratory synthesis identified only two studies with extractable knowledge outcome effect sizes, both implausibly large (g > 2.0), likely reflecting small-sample bias, absence of blinding, and practice effects.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The available evidence suggests that technology-enhanced teaching modalities are promising for HBOT education, but the field lacks methodologically rigorous comparative studies and no study yet demonstrates consistent superiority over traditional didactic teaching. The anomalously large effect sizes in the few quantitative studies signal a high risk of bias and an urgent need for adequately powered randomised trials with blinded outcome assessment, standardised outcome measures, and a consensus-derived competency framework.

articles.title: Focused Cardiac Ultrasound and Doppler Hemodynamics in Nephrology Practice.

abstract.text: Point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) in nephrology is evolving beyond kidney imaging and procedural guidance toward integrated hemodynamic assessment. Distinguishing reduced forward flow from elevated filling pressures and venous congestion remains challenging in patients with acute kidney injury and cardiorenal syndromes. This educational review discusses the clinical reasoning behind incorporating basic and advanced cardiac POCUS into nephrology practice. We highlight the interpretation and limitations of ventricular size and function, inferior vena cava assessment, stroke volume and left ventricular outflow tract Doppler, left ventricular filling pressures, right-sided and pulmonary artery pressures, and right ventricular outflow tract Doppler, with emphasis on how these findings may influence fluid removal, volume administration, and vasoactive therapy. The complementary role of venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) in assessing the downstream consequences of systemic venous congestion is also discussed. Rather than relying on isolated sonographic parameters or rigid cutoffs, cardiac POCUS findings should be integrated with multisystem ultrasound and the broader clinical context. Familiarity with these principles can help nephrologists obtain focused, repeatable hemodynamic information at the bedside and translate sonographic findings into more physiologically informed clinical decisions.

articles.title: Clinical Outcomes Associated With Intravenous Fluid Shortages in Emergency Department Patients: A Propensity Score Matched Cohort Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Intravenous (IV) saline is critical for emergency department (ED) care, supporting resuscitation, rehydration, and electrolyte correction. National IV fluid shortages, including the shortage following Hurricane Helene in September 2024, may disrupt timely care, yet large-scale evidence on associated clinical outcomes is limited.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this retrospective observational cohort study using the TriNetX global federated electronic health record network, adult ED patients aged 18-65 years presenting during a nationwide IV fluid shortage (October 2024-May 2025) were compared with those presenting during a prior period of adequate supply. Cohorts were propensity score matched on demographics and comorbidities. Time-to-event outcomes within 7 days were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards models.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: After matching, 2,767,318 patients were included in each cohort. Compared with the non-shortage period, ED visits during the shortage were associated with small but consistent increases in rates of sepsis (HR 1.066), gastroenteritis (HR 1.151), acute kidney failure (HR 1.006), and hyponatremia (HR 1.074). Fluid administration was reduced (HR 0.869), consistent with expectations during the shortage period. Hospitalization (HR 1.06) was more frequent, while mortality did not differ.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Nationwide IV fluid shortages were associated with mild increases in acute complications and healthcare utilization among ED patients without increased short-term mortality. These findings underscore the need for preparedness strategies to mitigate the clinical impact of future IV fluid supply disruptions. Effect sizes were modest, and while statistically significant, they likely represent small individual level clinical differences. Given the large number of ED encounters affected, these patterns may reflect broader health-system strain during the nationwide shortage.

articles.title: Frailty is associated with longer time to hemorrhage-control surgery after trauma.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Frailty is associated with adverse outcomes after trauma, but whether it is associated with the timeliness of operative hemorrhage control is unknown. We evaluated the association between frailty and time to initiation of hemorrhage-control surgery after traumatic injury.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the 2023-2024 American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Programs Participant Use Files. Adults undergoing hemorrhage-control surgery within 24 hours of arrival were included. Frailty was defined using the 5-factor modified frailty index, with a 5-factor modified frailty index ≥0.40 classified as frail. The primary outcome was time from hospital arrival to hemorrhage-control surgery initiation. Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood regression with robust standard errors was used to estimate adjusted mean time ratios, with age modeled using restricted cubic splines. Prespecified explanatory and sensitivity analyses evaluated physiologic urgency, preoperative computed tomography, age overlap, injury severity, procedure type, and extreme hemorrhage-control surgery times.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 29,762 patients, 1,804 (6.1%) were frail. Median hemorrhage-control surgery initiation time was 94.2 minutes (interquartile range, 46.2-190.8) in frail patients and 61.8 minutes (interquartile range, 34.2-126.0) in nonfrail patients (P < .001). After adjustment, frailty was associated with longer mean hemorrhage-control surgery initiation time (adjusted mean time ratio, 1.09; 95% confidence interval, 1.02-1.17; P = .007). Standardized adjusted mean times were 132.6 minutes for frail patients and 121.3 minutes for nonfrail patients, an adjusted difference of 11.3 minutes (95% confidence interval, 2.8-19.9). The association persisted after adjustment for physiologic urgency and preoperative computed tomography (adjusted mean time ratio, 1.08; 95% confidence interval, 1.02-1.16) and in age-restricted, blunt-trauma, direct emergency department-to-operating room, ≤360-minute, and median-regression analyses, although estimates were attenuated in Injury Severity Score ≥16 and laparotomy/pelvic-packing-only subgroups.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Frailty was independently associated with a longer time to hemorrhage-control surgery initiation after trauma, beyond chronological age and measured clinical characteristics. These findings identify frailty as a marker associated with the pathway to operative hemorrhage control but should not be interpreted as evidence of inappropriate delay or a causal effect of frailty on care.

articles.title: Young ERC Masterclass journal club article: intubation trends and survival in paediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest - a critical appraisal.
Intra-arrest blood pressure monitoring during paediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To evaluate the use of intra-arrest blood pressure monitoring and association between blood pressure thresholds and outcomes in infants and children.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A systematic review was performed, registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024590080). We executed the search strategy on MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials all years until April 1, 2026. We used GRADE and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale to assess the evidence found. Critically important outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital discharge, and survival with favourable neurological outcome, as defined in the Paediatric Core Outcome Set for Cardiac Arrest.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Six studies were included in the final analysis. Two studies (577 events) were pooled. A diastolic blood pressure (DBP) of ≥25 mmHg for infants <1 year and ≥30 mmHg for children 1-≤18 years, averaged over the first ten minutes of CPR, was associated with improved rates of ROSC, survival to hospital discharge, and survival with favourable neurological outcome, with very low certainty of evidence. The analysis did not find a statistically significant association for intra-arrest systolic blood pressure (SBP) thresholds and the described outcomes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In infants and children with invasive arterial monitoring in place during IHCA, a DBP of ≥25 mmHg (infants) or ≥30 mmHg (children) during the first 10 min of CPR was associated with improved survival and neurological outcome. The evidence is observational and of very low certainty, and does not establish that titrating resuscitation to these thresholds improves outcomes.The protocol for this systematic review was registered as PROSPERO ID CRD42024590080.

articles.title: Golden Hours in Disaster Response and Early Clinical Outcomes: An Analysis of the First 24 Hours of the Kahramanmaraş Earthquake.

abstract.text: Background: This study examined the association between admission time within 24 h of the Kahramanmaraş earthquakes and trauma severity, rhabdomyolysis, and in-hospital mortality, and its potential as a temporal reference for field triage in mass-casualty incidents. Methods: This retrospective study included earthquake-related injury patients who presented to our tertiary emergency department within 24 h of the earthquake onset (04:17, 6 February 2023). Non-survivors who died before diagnostic work-up, and therefore had no laboratory results or trauma scores, were excluded from the analysis. Patients were compared by admission within the golden hour (≤6 h) or later (>6 h); laboratory samples were obtained within the first hour of presentation. Mortality predictors were examined using univariate and multivariable logistic regression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis evaluated admission time for predicting rhabdomyolysis. Results: Three of 63 patients (4.8%) died; lower Glasgow Coma Scale scores and higher trauma severity indices were associated with mortality, whereas admission time and entrapment were not (very few deaths). Patients admitted after 6 h had higher Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) grades and significantly higher creatine kinase (CK), creatine kinase-MB isoenzyme (CK-MB), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), C-reactive protein (CRP), and international normalized ratio (INR) values and longer hospitalizations. Admission time predicted rhabdomyolysis well (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.840; cutoff: 9 h) and correlated positively with log-transformed CK (r = 0.733). Conclusions: The initial temporal window may be associated with muscle and organ injury severity among patients reaching hospital, but does not support redefining the golden hour as a survival determinant across the care continuum. The time threshold is hypothesis-generating and requires external validation before field triage use.

articles.title: Emergency Department-Centered Digital Health Transformation: Narrative Review and Three-Pillar Implementation Framework.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency departments (EDs) face escalating pressures from rising patient volumes, workforce shortages, and documentation burdens. Digital health technologies have shown promise individually, but most are implemented in isolation, limiting their collective impact. This narrative review synthesizes evidence for six digital health technologies applicable to the ED and proposes a three-pillar framework for their coordinated implementation, positioning the ED as a convergence point for health system digital transformation.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We searched PubMed and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed literature published from 2018 through July 2026 on ambient artificial intelligence (AI) documentation, telehospitalist programs, virtual nursing, remote patient monitoring, virtual specialty consultation, and postdischarge transitional care, prioritizing systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Fifty-one sources met inclusion criteria and were synthesized. We organized the technologies into three functional pillars: streamlining clinical workflows; expanding workforce capacity; and extending continuity of care. Outcomes included clinical, operational, and implementation measures. Experience from Houston Methodist, a nine-hospital health system, is presented as an illustrative example separate from the literature synthesis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the 51 sources, 23 (45.1%) addressed streamlining clinical workflows, 16 (31.4%) expanding workforce capacity, and 12 (23.5%) extending continuity of care. Overall, 22 (43.1%) were ED-specific: 10, five, and seven within the respective pillars. Ambient AI documentation included 13 sources (seven ED-specific); telestroke included one ED-specific source. Evidence maturity varied by technology and setting. In non-ED settings, meta-analyses reported shorter documentation time with ambient AI documentation (standardized mean difference, -0.72; 95% CI, -0.99 to -0.45), lower hospital mortality with tele-intensive care (risk ratio, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.58-0.96), and lower odds of 30-day readmission with low-complexity post-discharge interventions (odds ratio [OR], 0.78; 95% CI, 0.66-0.92). Emergency department-specific evidence remained largely observational; one meta-analysis showed no mortality difference with telestroke (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 0.94-1.43), while one systematic review found no demonstrable benefits from telephone follow-up post-ED discharge.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Current evidence supports individual digital health technologies in and around the ED. Based on implementation science principles and institutional experience, we propose that coordinated implementation across the three pillars may offer advantages over isolated deployments, a hypothesis warranting prospective comparative evaluation.

articles.title: [Delayed diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome in a patient with psychiatric illness].

abstract.text: In this case report, a 24-year-old woman diagnosed with psychiatric disorders such as anxiety, OCD and presumably a schizotypical disorder presented with symptoms of Guillain-Barré syndrome. The patient had a history of somatisation, which is why her symptoms were initially overlooked. After several contacts to the emergency department, the patient was hospitalised after finding bilateral lung embolisms. The patient deteriorated quickly and suffered shortly from hypoxic cardiac arrest. Whilst she was in the ICU, she was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome.

articles.title: Association of the ISAR Score with Clinical and Operational Outcomes in Older Emergency Department Patients.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: The Identification of Seniors at Risk (ISAR) score is widely used to identify older emergency department (ED) patients at increased risk of adverse outcomes. However, its association with immediate disposition and operational outcomes remains incompletely characterized. This study evaluated the association of ISAR scores with hospital admission and emergency department length of stay (EDLOS). Methods: This retrospective observational cohort study included ED presentations of patients aged ≥65 years at a tertiary university emergency department in 2024. Of 12,105 eligible presentations, 10,090 (83.4%) had a documented ISAR score and constituted the descriptive cohort; 9401 presentations with classifiable admission status were included in the primary admission analysis. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, presenting complaint, triage category, treating specialty, and referral source. The incremental contribution of ISAR beyond routinely available clinical variables was assessed by nested model comparison and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Prolonged EDLOS was defined as ≥6 h. Results: Higher ISAR scores were independently associated with hospital admission and prolonged EDLOS. In the continuous-score admission model, each one-point increase in ISAR was associated with higher odds of admission (OR 1.155, 95% CI 1.121-1.191; p < 0.001), although categorical sensitivity analysis demonstrated a nonlinear association with a plateau at higher scores. ISAR alone showed modest discrimination for admission (AUC 0.589, 95% CI 0.577-0.600). Addition of ISAR to the clinical model increased the AUC from 0.696 to 0.705 (ΔAUC = 0.009, 95% CI 0.005-0.012; p < 0.001). Median EDLOS increased from 326 min (IQR 215-494) at ISAR 0 to 596 min (IQR 324-1312) at ISAR 6. After adjustment including hospital admission status, each one-point increase in ISAR was associated with higher odds of prolonged EDLOS (OR 1.178, 95% CI 1.143-1.214; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Higher ISAR scores were associated with both hospital admission and prolonged EDLOS. ISAR provided statistically significant but modest incremental prognostic information beyond routinely available clinical variables and should be regarded as a geriatric risk-screening tool rather than a stand-alone disposition instrument. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether ISAR-guided clinical pathways improve patient or operational outcomes.

articles.title: Associations of Secondary Traumatic Stress and Emotional Labor with Suicidal Ideation Among Emergency Dispatch Personnel in South Korea: A Cross-Sectional Moderated Mediation Analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency dispatch personnel are repeatedly exposed to callers' distress and emotionally demanding interactions, yet suicidal ideation in this workforce remains understudied. This study examined associations of secondary traumatic stress (STS) and emotional labor with suicidal ideation, including indirect associations through depression and conditional associations involving social support.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A cross-sectional correlational study was conducted among 211 fire-service personnel assigned to emergency dispatch centers in Busan and Gyeongnam, South Korea. Data were analyzed using Hayes' PROCESS macro Model 59 with HC3 standard errors and 5000 bootstrap resamples.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Social support moderated the associations of STS with depression and suicidal ideation and the association of depression with suicidal ideation. The conditional indirect association of STS with suicidal ideation through depression decreased across low, mean, and high social support (0.191, 0.076, and 0.013). For emotional labor, the emotional labor × social support interaction was significant in the depression model, and its association with depression and indirect association with suicidal ideation through depression were supported at low and mean, but not high, social support.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: STS and depression were associated with suicidal ideation, and the indirect association of STS through depression was weaker at higher social support. However, moderation findings involving suicidal ideation should be interpreted cautiously because the corresponding interaction terms were not statistically significant in the Tobit sensitivity analysis.

articles.title: Shoulder Dislocation Reduction Using Inhaled Nitrous Oxide in the Emergency Department: Retrospective Case Series.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Inhaled nitrous oxide (iNO) offers rapid onset analgesia with a favorable safety profile yet remains underused for shoulder dislocation reductions in the emergency department (ED). The objective of this study was to evaluate the use and outcomes of iNO for shoulder reduction in the ED, including whether intravenous (IV) access was required, whether successful reduction could be accomplished without additional analgesic or sedative medications under procedural sedation, and the rate of adverse effects from iNO.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective chart review of shoulder dislocation reductions using iNO at two high-volume EDs over three years (2019-2022). Data collected included age, sex, indication, procedural success, IV placement, medications administered, and adverse events and was stored in a password-protected database. The primary endpoint was successful reduction with iNO as the primary procedural analgesic; secondary endpoint was occurrence of any adverse events.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 138 patients, 125 (90.6%; 95% CI, 0.84-0.95) achieved successful reduction with iNO alone without escalation to procedural sedation; 102 patients (74%) did not require IV access. Adverse events were rare (2/138 or 1.4% [95% CI, 0.02-0.05]): one patient experienced transient agitation (a known side effect of N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonism), and one had vomiting. Both were self-limited without hemodynamic changes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This retrospective case series, the largest of its kind to date examining iNO for shoulder dislocation reduction, demonstrated a 90.6% success rate with minimal adverse events and reduced resource utilization compared to procedural sedation. These findings support further prospective investigation of iNO for shoulder dislocation as well as other orthopedic reductions and painful ED procedures.

articles.title: Effects of Racial Concordance and Perceived Racism on Emergency Department Patient Satisfaction.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Racial disparities in healthcare persist, with evidence suggesting that bias contributes to inequities in care and outcomes for Black patients. Racial concordance between patients and clinicians has been proposed as one strategy to improve patient satisfaction and health outcomes, but its impact in acute care settings such as the emergency department (ED) remains underexplored. The objective of this study was to assess how racial concordance between patient and clinician, together with patient perceptions of how race affected their care, influence patient satisfaction with care in the ED.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This secondary analysis used data from a previously published text message-based survey of patients discharged from two EDs between August and September 2021. Patients were categorized as not completely discordant if at least one clinician (physician, advanced practice clinician, or nurse) shared their self-identified race. The primary outcome was patient ratings of experience with ED care (scored 0 = poor to 5 = excellent). Multivariable ordinal logistic regression was used to assess associations between racial concordance, perceived impact of race on care, and experience ratings.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 516 respondents, 195 (37.8%) were classified as not completely discordant with at least one emergency clinician. Not completely discordant patients reported significantly lower experience ratings (scored 0 to 5) compared to racially discordant patients (median, 4 [3-5] vs 5 [3-5]; P = .01). In multivariable ordinal logistic regression, racial concordance was not independently significant in patient experience.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Contrary to expectations, in our population, racial concordance was not significantly associated with satisfaction in ED care. In the adjusted analysis, perceived negative impact on care due to race was the strongest independent predictor of lower overall satisfaction. These findings suggest that how patients perceived the role of race in their care may be more influential than simply patient-clinician concordance in the acute care setting. Further research is needed to investigate these factors in more diverse patient-clinician population and other ED settings to help inform policies focused on advancing health equity.

articles.title: English versus Non-English Language Preference and Computed Tomography Use in Pediatric Minor Head Trauma.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Whether the use of computed tomography (CT) in pediatric minor head trauma varies by documented language preference (English vs non-English), independent of race, is not well understood. Our objective was to identify factors associated with head CT use among children with minor head trauma in an institutional Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN)-based pathway.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients 2 to 14 years of age presenting with minor head trauma, January 2019 to June 2022, who were classified as low, intermediate, or high risk using PECARN criteria. Our primary outcome measure was a three-level clinical pathway: no CT and no traumatic brain injury (TBI); clinical TBI without CT; or CT performed. Secondary outcomes were CT positivity and short-term clinical outcomes. Multinomial logistic regression assessed associations between pathway and language preference, age, headache, weighted observed symptom score (OSS), and race (White vs non-White).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 1,167 patients, 319 (27.3%) underwent CT, 132 (11.3%) had clinical TBI diagnosis without CT, and 716 (61.4%) had neither; 430 (36.8%) were classified intermediate risk-the subgroup in which the imaging decision is most discretionary. Non-English language preference was associated with lower adjusted odds of CT in the intermediate-risk subgroup (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.24-0.92; P = .03) but not in the full cohort (aOR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.50-1.22; P = .27). Within the intermediate-risk subgroup, OSS was strongly associated with CT use (aOR, 3.65; 95% CI, 2.67-5.00; P < .001) and headache with clinical TBI without CT (aOR, 4.94; 95% CI, 1.64-14.90; P = .005), whereas race was not independently associated with CT use (aOR, 1.36; 95% CI, 0.82-2.25; P = .48). Language preference was not associated with CT positivity among scanned patients (aOR, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.44-2.72; P = .84), and short-term outcomes did not differ by language (all P > .35).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Documented non-English language preference was independently associated with lower use of head CT in PECARN intermediate-risk children; race was not after adjustment for clinical severity. Yield and short-term outcomes did not differ by language preference among imaged patients; however, imaging selection precludes conclusions about mechanism.

articles.title: Common Inpatient Procedures-Urinary Catheter Insertion and Intra-abdominal Pressure Measurement.
articles.journal_full: The Medical clinics of North America

abstract.text: This review provides a comprehensive guide to indwelling urinary catheterization and transvesicular intra-abdominal pressure measurement. It details essential anatomy, evidence-based insertion techniques for male and female patients, and the appropriate selection of catheter to minimize complications such as catheter-associated urinary tract infection and trauma. Furthermore, it highlights the integration of point-of-care ultrasound for troubleshooting and bladder volume assessment. By standardizing procedural steps and providing mitigation strategies for high-risk patients, this article aims to improve procedural success and enhance patient safety.

articles.title: Nerve Blocks.
articles.journal_full: The Medical clinics of North America

abstract.text: This article provides a clinical framework for implementing point-of-care blocks, distinguishing between precision-target and volume-dependent planar techniques for conditions like hip fractures and thoracic trauma. By focusing on sonographic anatomy, procedural ergonomics, and standardized safety protocols, the text outlines strategies to mitigate risks like Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity. Integrating New York School of Regional Anesthesia-standardized methodologies, the article emphasizes improving functional recovery through anatomy-driven, opioid-sparing interventions.

articles.title: Paracentesis.
articles.journal_full: The Medical clinics of North America

abstract.text: Abdominal paracentesis is a fundamental procedure for diagnosing ascitic etiologies and providing therapeutic relief for symptomatic tense ascites. The application of point-of-care ultrasound is the standard of care and enhances procedural success and minimizes complications such as hemorrhage or bowel perforation. While there are guidelines to help optimize bleeding diathesis, the clinician must perform an individual risk assessment and exercise sound clinical judgment to determine the optimal procedure approach to minimize bleeding complications. For large-volume paracentesis exceeding 5 L, albumin replacement (6-8 g per liter removed) is essential to mitigate postparacentesis circulatory dysfunction and acute kidney injury.

articles.title: Disaster Management and National Incident Management System.
articles.journal_full: The Surgical clinics of North America

abstract.text: Disasters overwhelm community and health care resources and are increasing in frequency and complexity. General surgeons play a critical role in disaster response, providing life-saving surgical care, participating in triage, and allocating scarce resources. Disaster management follows a continuous cycle of mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery, with health care systems emphasizing risk assessment, training, and surge planning. Effective response requires coordinated communication and resource management. The National Incident Management System provides a standardized framework for multiagency disaster response, incorporating the Incident Command System, Emergency Operations Centers, and coordinated communication structures to ensure organized, efficient, and scalable management.

articles.title: Co-Evolutionary Sensor Deployment Optimization for Layered Low-Altitude Airspace Monitoring Under Worst-Case Traffic Composition.

abstract.text: Layered sensor networks that monitor low-altitude airspace must detect heterogeneous aerial traffic, yet sensor deployment is usually optimized against a single fixed traffic case and can leave an entire target kind undetected when the composition changes. This paper formulates deployment against worst-case traffic composition through a high-low transition (HL) trajectory model, a library of 35 target templates in four kinds, and a per-kind fairness objective f4, the worst per-kind miss rate. An adaptive co-evolution (ACE) framework trains deployments against a co-evolved, kind-diverse population of traffic cases with a hall of fame and a robust final selection, and ACE-A6 instantiates it with a sensor-count dispatcher. Over four scenarios with five, four, three, and two sensors; 30 seeds; and two independent sets of 60 held-out cases, ACE-A6 lowers the worst per-kind miss rate of four state-of-the-art evolutionary optimizers on the four-, three- and two-sensor scenarios with large effect sizes (Cliff's δ≥ 0.44, Holm-corrected p<0.05). Equal-budget experiments locate the gain in the training framework: each of five optimizers trained inside ACE breaks the f4,max=1 ceiling, and ACE-A6 performs on par with them. The advantage persists under probabilistic detection, masking, position error and moderate library shift.

articles.title: Workplace Violence Exposure and Burnout Among Fire-Service-Based Paramedics in South Korea: The Indirect Association Through Post-Traumatic Stress Symptoms and the Moderating Roles of Social Support and Resilience.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: This study examined the indirect association between workplace violence exposure and burnout through post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) and the moderating roles of social support and resilience among South Korean fire-service-based paramedics. Methods: This analytical cross-sectional study included 210 paramedics in Busan, South Korea. Conditional process analyses were conducted using PROCESS Model 8, with social support and resilience examined in separate models. Results: Workplace violence exposure was positively associated with PTSS, which was positively associated with burnout. Conditional indirect associations were significant at the mean of each moderator. In the final sample (N = 210), social support moderated the associations of workplace violence exposure with PTSS (p = 0.002) and burnout (p = 0.015), and its index of moderated mediation was significant (-0.024, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.041, -0.009]). However, the social support interaction predicting PTSS and its index of moderated mediation were statistically significant only after excluding one influential observation (N = 210 vs. N = 211). The social support interaction predicting burnout remained significant in both samples. Resilience did not significantly moderate the PTSS association; its nominally significant interaction predicting burnout did not remain significant after Holm correction, and its index of moderated mediation was not significant. Conclusions: Social support may play a moderating role in the associations linking workplace violence exposure, PTSS, and burnout, although some findings were sensitive to the exclusion of one influential observation. These cross-sectional findings require cautious interpretation and further replication.

articles.title: Improving Access to Specialty Care: Analysis of Factors Affecting Follow-up Patterns in an Outpatient Academic Pulmonary Clinic.

abstract.text: Prolonged wait times for appointments in pulmonary specialty clinics contribute to worse patient outcomes. We determined the follow-up patterns and factors associated with appointment no-show to identify opportunities to increase appointment availability while improving follow-up. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of patients scheduled from 2017-2019 in the outpatient pulmonary fellows' clinic of an academic tertiary care hospital.
