A successful visit was an appointment documented as completed. Appointment-level associations with no-show were evaluated using multivariable logistic generalized estimating equations. Among 1,612 patients, 4,689 appointments were scheduled. After excluding 1,247 cancellations and 6 appointments with indeterminate disposition, 3,436 appointments among 1,479 patients were included in the no-show analysis; 1,461 (42.5%) were no-shows. Average intended and actual follow-up intervals were 11.2 weeks and 24.8 weeks, respectively. In the complete-case adjusted analysis (3,427 appointments among 1,470 patients), substance use disorders (adjusted odds ratios [aORs], 1.86-3.43; P≤.011), inpatient referral (aOR, 2.41; P<.001), and pneumonia (aOR, 2.63; P=.046) were associated with greater odds of no-show. Spanish language (aOR, 0.59; P<.001), charity care (aOR, 0.63; P=.002), and external outpatient referral (aOR, 0.49; P<.001) were associated with lower odds. Emergency department referral and driving distance were not independently associated with no-show. Our clinic had short intended follow-up intervals and a high no-show rate. These appointment-level associations may inform continuity-focused scheduling and targeted attendance support. Standardizing follow-up intervals and using prediction-based overbooking should be prospectively evaluated for effects on access, workflow, and patient experience.

articles.title: Central Venous Access.
articles.journal_full: The Medical clinics of North America

abstract.text: Central venous catheterization (CVC) is a commonly performed procedure in which an indwelling catheter is placed within a central vein to facilitate administration of vasoactive medications, chemotherapy, parenteral nutrition, and extracorporeal therapies, as well as hemodynamic monitoring. This article reviews the indications and contraindications for CVC placement, bleeding risk considerations, and factors influencing site selection. Methods for confirming catheter position, including sonographic and radiographic approaches, are discussed. Mechanical, thrombotic, and infectious complications are reviewed, along with strategies for prevention and postprocedural monitoring. Common technical and sonographic pitfalls encountered during CVC placement are also highlighted.

articles.title: Safety and Analgesic Consumption Impact of Continuous Peripheral Regional Analgesia in Earthquake-Related Crush Injury: A Retrospective Cohort Study.

abstract.text: Background: The 6 February 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake caused an unprecedented burden of crush-related extremity trauma. Continuous peripheral regional analgesia is frequently used in these patients, but its safety regarding renal outcomes and its effect on systemic opioid consumption have not been quantified in comparative cohort data. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, exploratory cohort study of 181 hospitalizations (141 patients) following the earthquake, comparing patients who received a continuous peripheral nerve catheter with those managed without one. No prospective sample-size calculation was performed. The primary outcome was acute kidney injury (AKI), defined per adapted KDIGO criteria; the secondary outcome was systemic opioid exposure, assessed both as opioid-days and, in a dose-based sensitivity analysis, as morphine milligram equivalents (MME). Because patients contributed multiple admissions, regression models used cluster-robust standard errors. A propensity-score-matched sensitivity analysis (age, sex) addressed confounding by indication, and intensive care unit (ICU) days were added as a further covariate in sensitivity models. Results: Catheter and non-catheter groups had similar age (p = 0.369) but differed in length of stay (median 42 vs. 16 days) and surgical procedures (10 vs. 2), reflecting catheter-selection criteria; detailed injury-severity and comorbidity data were not available for either group. Catheter use was not significantly associated with AKI (adjusted OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.16-1.47, p = 0.203) or with systemic opioid-day rate (adjusted RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.88-1.51, p = 0.294). Results were materially unchanged after adding ICU days as a covariate (AKI OR 0.42, p = 0.148, n = 123; opioid-days RR 1.23, p = 0.223, n = 160) and when opioid exposure was expressed as MME per day (adjusted ratio 1.32, 95% CI 0.73-2.38, p = 0.361, n = 165). A propensity-matched analysis (26 pairs) was concordant for all outcomes. Conclusions: In this exploratory, hypothesis-generating cohort, we did not detect a significant association between continuous regional analgesia and either AKI risk or opioid consumption across six complementary analyses. These non-significant findings do not establish equivalence or safety, particularly given wide confidence intervals, a modest number of events, incomplete clinical characterization, and residual confounding that could not be fully resolved with the available data; they should be regarded as hypothesis-generating pending confirmation in better-characterized, adequately powered, multicenter cohorts.

articles.title: Redundancy-Based Validity Screening of Strain-Gauge Records from In-Service Hydraulic Turbine Servomotors.

abstract.text: Strain gauges on the push-pull rod are a practical means of measuring the load on in-service hydraulic actuators, but the channels degrade silently, and a degraded channel still yields a credible-looking load characteristic. A redundancy-based validity screen for such records is presented and applied to every record from four guide-vane servomotors of Francis units under wind-photovoltaic-hydro complementary dispatch. Four elementary screens are combined: channel coherence with an applicability floor, configuration sensitivity of the interval loading gradient against a tolerance band built from fifteen reference channel configurations, step magnitude, and abscissa integrity. The screen refuses none of the reference configurations, in sample or under leave-one-out. At a three-channel actuator it localises a disagreement to one gauge; at a two-channel actuator it can only detect one, and it refuses a record whose loading gradient, -310 kN per unit relative opening, lies 365 kN below the reference range. For records that pass, loop energy is expressed through a stroke-free dissipation index and a growth rate. The channel configuration carried forward at a single actuator moves the cross-actuator coefficient of variation in the index between 6.6% and 20.8%, whereas the grouping by growth rate is preserved for every configuration that excludes the isolated gauge.

articles.title: Burnout in Out-of-Hospital Emergency Healthcare Professionals: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon that particularly affects healthcare professionals exposed to sustained stress. In out-of-hospital emergency care, repeated exposure to critical incidents, violence, and demanding shift patterns may increase this risk. This review aimed to estimate the prevalence of burnout dimensions and identify factors associated with burnout among prehospital emergency care professionals. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261489417). CINAHL, LILACS, PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched in July 2026. Quantitative studies that measured burnout with the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) or the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI) were included. Prevalences were pooled using random-effects models, and the certainty of the evidence was rated with GRADE. Results: Thirty-one studies (9926 unique participants) were included, 12 of which contributed to the meta-analyses. The pooled prevalence was 33% (95% CI 22-45%; I2 = 97.7%) for high emotional exhaustion, 37% (95% CI 26-48%; I2 = 97.1%) for high depersonalization and 27% (95% CI 17-38%; I2 = 97.4%) for low personal accomplishment, with overlapping confidence intervals and wide prediction intervals. The most consistent associated factors were exposure to workplace violence, lack of organizational and supervisor support, and demanding shift patterns; findings for professional role, gender, age, and years of experience were mixed. The certainty of the pooled estimates was very low. Conclusions: Around one in three prehospital professionals shows high levels in each burnout dimension, although estimates vary widely between settings. Organizational strategies focused on violence prevention, supervisory support, and early detection are needed.

articles.title: Workflow and Clinical Outcomes After Implementation of a Structured Trauma Protocol in a Resource-Constrained Emergency Department: A Single-Center Retrospective Before-and-After Cohort Study.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Coordinated imaging and clinical decision-making are central to trauma care, but delays may occur in emergency departments without hybrid resuscitation-imaging facilities. We examined associations between a structured departmental quality-improvement workflow and trauma-process times in a resource-constrained emergency department. Methods: We retrospectively compared 360 consecutive eligible trauma patients (180 before and 180 after implementation). The post-protocol workflow combined early extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST), prioritized computed tomography (CT) coordination, and brief post-resuscitation debriefing. The primary outcome was CT access time. Other workflow outcomes were evaluated as secondary endpoints; procedural and mortality findings were exploratory. Results: Median CT access time was 22.38 min (IQR 16.02-28.75) before implementation and 10.98 min (IQR 7.53-14.71) afterward (p < 0.001); the mean difference was -11.10 min (95% CI -12.69 to -9.50). Median consultation-request time was 23.23 versus 13.69 min, and median admission-decision time was 125.95 versus 49.08 min (both p < 0.001). Pre-CT tube thoracostomy was recorded more often in the post-protocol phase (3.3% vs. 11.7%; RR 3.50, 95% CI 1.45-8.47; p = 0.003). Differences in mortality were exploratory and cannot be attributed to the protocol. Conclusions: The post-protocol phase was associated with shorter trauma workflow intervals, particularly CT access time. Because this retrospective, uncontrolled comparison followed calendar sequence, it cannot establish a causal protocol effect. Procedural and mortality findings are hypothesis-generating; controlled studies are needed to assess reproducibility and patient-centered benefit.

articles.title: Continuous Near-Infrared Spectroscopy as a Real-Time Monitor of Intravenous Thrombolysis in Acute Ischaemic Stroke: A Prospective Observational Emergency Department Study.

abstract.text: Background. Intravenous (IV) thrombolysis is the standard of care for acute ischaemic stroke (AIS), yet there is still no objective bedside tool for monitoring the brain continuously during the infusion. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) provides non-invasive, continuous measurement of regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO2). We evaluated whether bilateral frontal NIRS, and in particular the absolute interhemispheric difference in rSO2 (ΔNIRS), tracks the clinical trajectory of patients receiving IV alteplase in the emergency department (ED). Methods. A prospective observational cohort study was conducted in the ED of a tertiary university hospital. Consecutive adults receiving IV alteplase for AIS were screened, and those enrolled underwent continuous bilateral frontal NIRS monitoring. Bilateral rSO2, ΔNIRS, vital signs, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) were recorded at baseline and at 0, 15, 30, 45, 60 and 120 min after the start of the infusion. Patients were classified by clinical trajectory during monitoring as improvement, no change, or deterioration. Results. Forty-one patients were analyzed (26 female, 63.4%; mean age 73.6 ± 14.8 years); 15 (36.6%) improved, 21 (51.2%) showed no change and 5 (12.2%) deteriorated. In the whole cohort, absolute rSO2 rose only slightly in the affected hemisphere and did not change in the unaffected hemisphere. However, affected-hemisphere rSO2 rose significantly in the improvement group (median 59 to 67; p = 0.001) and fell significantly in the deterioration group (p = 0.015). ΔNIRS narrowed from a median of 4 (IQR 3-9) at baseline to 1 (IQR 0-5) at 120 min in the improvement group (p = 0.034) and did not change significantly in the other groups. The two patients with acute complications desaturated bilaterally. NIHSS correlated strongly and inversely with GCS at every time point (ρ = -0.74 to -0.84; all p < 0.001). Conclusions. During IV thrombolysis in the ED, continuous bilateral frontal NIRS tracked the clinical trajectory. Because recanalisation and reperfusion were not assessed independently, what NIRS paralleled was the clinical course, not reperfusion itself. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant larger studies that validate ΔNIRS against perfusion or vascular imaging.

articles.title: Geographic access, prehospital delay, and testicular loss in pediatric testicular torsion.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate the association between geographic access, prehospital and in-hospital treatment delays, and orchiectomy in children undergoing surgery for testicular torsion.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a retrospective cohort study of pediatric patients with surgically confirmed testicular torsion between 2020 and 2025. The surgical outcome was orchiectomy versus orchidopexy at the index operation. Geographic access was assessed using estimated home-to-hospital driving time and driving distance based on residential ZIP code. Prehospital and in-hospital intervals and interfacility transfer were also evaluated. To reduce the influence of prolonged symptom duration on the assessment of geographic access, geographic analyses were additionally restricted to patients with an exact symptom-to-arrival time of ≤24 h, with ≤12 h evaluated as a sensitivity analysis. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate associations with orchiectomy.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 131 patients were included; 76 (58.0%) underwent orchiectomy and 55 (42.0%) underwent orchidopexy. In the overall cohort, median symptom-to-arrival time was substantially longer among patients undergoing orchiectomy than among those undergoing orchidopexy (2700 vs 360 min; p < 0.001). Among patients presenting within 24 h (n = 73), symptom-to-arrival time did not differ significantly between the orchiectomy and orchidopexy groups (449 vs 335 min; p = 0.360), whereas estimated driving time was longer among patients undergoing orchiectomy (70 vs 31 min; p = 0.023). After adjustment for age, each additional 30 min of estimated driving time was associated with higher odds of orchiectomy (aOR 1.39, 95% CI 1.05-1.83; p = 0.021). The association was attenuated after additional adjustment for interfacility transfer. A ≤12-h sensitivity analysis showed a similar direction of association, although estimates were less precise.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Prehospital symptom duration was strongly associated with surgical outcome in the overall cohort. Among patients presenting within 24 h, longer estimated driving time was associated with orchiectomy after adjustment for age, although the association was attenuated after accounting for interfacility transfer. These findings suggest that geographic access may contribute to the prehospital care pathway among early presenters, while highlighting the importance of symptom duration and referral pathways in interpreting this association.

articles.title: Head Impacts in Long-Term Care Falls Are Common but Often Underrecognized: A Video-Based Analysis of Injury and Transport.

abstract.text: Falls are the leading cause of injury-related morbidity and mortality among older adults, particularly in long-term care (LTC) facilities. Although head impacts are common during falls, the relationship between impact occurrence, injury characteristics, and hospital transport remains inadequately defined. The objectives of this study were to (1) compare falls with and without head impact, (2) quantify unrecognized head impacts and their contexts, (3) examine factors associated with head injury occurrence, and (4) identify predictors of hospital transport following head impacts. This secondary analysis used an open-source video dataset from two LTC facilities. Three raters reviewed each of the 300 fall videos to determine the presence of head impact. Transport and injury data were extracted directly from the open-source, observational video dataset. Falls were characterized using the Fall Video Analysis Questionnaire. Generalized estimating equations evaluated predictors of head injury, and logistic regression modeled predictors of hospital transport. Head impacts were common yet often underrecognized when relying on reported or visible injuries. Many falls without documented head injury demonstrated clear head impact on video, indicating that visible injury is a poor proxy for impact. Hospital transport following head impact was uncommon and was primarily associated with visible injuries rather than patient characteristics or fall history. Most head impacts, including those without obvious injury, did not result in transport. These findings suggest that reliance on external injury may lead to underrecognition and potential under-triage of head trauma. Improved detection strategies beyond visible injury are needed to better identify clinically significant head impacts.

articles.title: Intrathecal hyperbaric versus isobaric bupivacaine for caesarean delivery: A meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND AIMS
abstract.text: Intrathecal bupivacaine facilitates caesarean delivery and is available in two forms: isobaric or hyperbaric with differing pharmacokinetic profiles. This meta-analysis primarily aimed to compare the incidence of hypotension (defined as a drop ≥20% from baseline systolic or mean arterial pressure) when used in caesarean delivery.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intrathecal isobaric and hyperbaric bupivacaine for caesarean delivery were identified from MEDLINE, Google Scholar, and Cochrane databases. Secondary outcomes included incidence of ephedrine use, nausea/vomiting, bradycardia, maximum block height, time to maximum block height, and offset of block. Jadad scores evaluated the trials' quality. RevMan statistical software® calculated the standardised mean difference with 95% confidence intervals for continuous variables. The Mantel-Haenszel test and a random effect model were used to calculate the odds ratio for dichotomous variables. Included articles were assessed for risk of bias and consistency with Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation guidelines.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Nineteen articles with 1501 patients were analysed with 722 patients receiving isobaric bupivacaine versus 779 receiving hyperbaric bupivacaine. There was no significant difference in the rates of hypotension [odds ratio (OR) 1.25, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.63 to 2.46] or incidence of ephedrine use (OR 1.44, 95% CI 0.75 to 2.77). There was a faster onset of motor block with hyperbaric bupivacaine (standardised mean difference -0.46, 95% CI -0.86 to -0.05) but no other differences in secondary outcomes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Despite differences between isobaric and hyperbaric bupivacaine, neither caused a significantly higher incidence of hypotension. Both produce similar clinical profiles except for onset of motor block. High levels of heterogeneity between the studies indicate the need for focused RCTs on this topic.

articles.title: ROX vs. HACOR: early prediction of HFNC failure in ICU patients admitted from the emergency department with lung cancer-related hypoxemia.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Delayed intubation in lung cancer patients receiving high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy is associated with increased mortality. Reliable bedside tools are essential for early risk stratification. We aimed to compare the predictive performance of the ROX index and HACOR score for the early identification of HFNC failure in this high-risk population.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective observational study included 176 ICU patients with lung cancer and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure who received HFNC. Time-point analyses of the ROX index and HACOR score at 1 and 3 h were restricted to patients with complete physiological data at both time points (n = 88). The primary outcome was clinician-determined HFNC failure, defined as endotracheal intubation within 48 h after HFNC initiation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: HFNC failure occurred in 50 of 176 patients (28.4%) in the overall cohort and in 39 of 88 patients (44.3%) in the complete-case analytical cohort. Patients who required endotracheal intubation exhibited higher baseline illness severity (SOFA and APACHE II) and persistent tachypnea. At the 3-hour assessment, the ROX index showed higher observed discrimination than the HACOR score (AUROC 0.860 [95% CI 0.760-0.960] vs. 0.740 [95% CI 0.590-0.890]). Only the prespecified 1- and 3-hour time points were evaluated; therefore, these findings do not establish 3 h as the optimal assessment time. In an exploratory analysis in which the threshold was derived and evaluated in the same analytical cohort, a 3-hour ROX value ≤ 5.1 identified patients at higher risk of HFNC failure; this threshold has not been independently validated. Respiratory rate alone also showed high prognostic value at 3 h (AUROC 0.850 [95% CI 0.730-0.970]).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Within the complete-case cohort, which represented half of the overall population, the 3-hour ROX index showed higher observed discrimination for clinician-determined HFNC failure than HACOR. However, selection and incorporation bias may have affected this comparison. The data-derived threshold should not be used as a stand-alone intubation criterion and requires prospective validation using standardized serial measurements and independently adjudicated outcomes.

abstract.label: CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: Not applicable; this was a retrospective observational study.

articles.title: Modelled Response Times for Police and Fire Brigade Co-Dispatch to Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Geospatial Simulation Study in Vorarlberg, Austria.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) depends on the interval between collapse and the start of chest compressions. We estimated how co-dispatching police and volunteer fire brigades alongside emergency medical services (EMS) would change the modelled time from dispatch to arrival of the first unit in Vorarlberg, Austria. Methods: In a geospatial simulation, 500 OHCA locations were drawn from a 100 m population raster, weighted by residential population. Driving times from all 18 EMS, 28 police and 121 volunteer fire stations were routed on the road network, and turnout times of 2 min (EMS), 0 min (police) and 5 min (fire brigade) were added; all units were modelled as continuously available at fixed stations. Four configurations (EMS alone, EMS plus police, EMS plus fire brigade, triple dispatch) were compared by paired time gains and 10 min coverage with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs); uncertainty from sampling, turnout times, unit availability and routing was assessed separately. Results: Of 500 missions, 499 were analysable. Median response time was 9.81 min with EMS alone, 5.45 min with EMS plus police, 7.36 min with EMS plus fire brigade and 5.41 min with triple dispatch; the paired median time gain of triple dispatch over EMS alone was 4.34 min (95% CI 3.80-4.67). Locations reached within 10 min rose from 51.1% to 87.4%, 87.0% and 94.6%, and the resident population inside the 10 min isochrones rose from 55.6% to 90.9%, 91.9% and 95.5%. Conclusions: Under fixed station locations, continuous unit availability and assumed agency-specific turnout times, police and fire brigade co-dispatch increased modelled ten-minute coverage compared with EMS alone. Police arrived earlier at most locations, whereas the denser fire station network contributed most in rural areas; their combination reached the most locations. Operational validation is required before these estimates can inform regional implementation.

articles.title: Diagnostic Value of Combined Biomarkers and the Shock Index for Predicting Febrile Neutropenia and Clinical Outcomes in the Emergency Department: A Multivariate Regression Analysis.

abstract.text: Background: Early risk stratification of febrile neutropenia (FN) in the emergency department (ED) is vital to accelerate empirical antibiotic management. This study evaluates the independent diagnostic performance of combined blood-borne inflammatory indices and the Shock Index (SI) in predicting FN status and severe clinical outcomes. Methods: Medical records of 338 febrile oncology patients presenting to the ED between 2020 and 2026 were retrospectively evaluated. Patients were divided into the FN group (fever + ANC < 1000 cells/μL; n = 213) and the control group (n = 125). Advanced cell-line metrics and biochemical ratios were calculated at admission. Independent predictors were isolated using multivariable logistic regression analysis. Results: Multivariable regression analysis revealed that elevated core body temperature (aOR: 3.229, 95% CI: 1.845-5.652, p < 0.001), lower serum sodium levels (aOR: 0.843, 95% CI: 0.767-0.926, p < 0.001), a low Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio (NLR) (aOR: 0.636, 95% CI: 0.549-0.736, p < 0.001), and an elevated Shock Index (aOR: 24.010, 95% CI: 2.258-255.360, p = 0.008) were stable independent predictors of FN. The combined four-variable integrated model achieved an outstanding Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.906 (95% CI: 0.874-0.937) with a diagnostic sensitivity of 77.4% and a specificity of 87.0%. Conclusions: Integrating baseline core temperature, hyponatremia, low cellular NLR, and physiologic SI values creates a rapid, cost-effective, and highly accurate screening platform to optimize emergency triage workflows and prevent computational delivery latency in critical oncologic emergencies.

articles.title: The Impact of Selected Physical Factors on Neurogenesis-What Do We Know?

abstract.text: New discoveries are constantly being made regarding cognitive processes, pain perception, the development of degenerative diseases, brain aging, and many other functions of the nervous system. Neurogenesis plays a significant role in all of these processes. As a manifestation of brain plasticity, neurogenesis continues throughout life, and its intensity can vary depending on internal and external factors. The process by which neurons are generated can be disrupted. This depends, among other things, on age and represents one of the potential targets for interventions aimed at improving cognitive function. Inhibition of neurogenesis increases the risk of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and other conditions that lead to dependence on others in their advanced stages. The status of the neurogenesis process can be monitored by measuring the levels of mediators in the blood. The state of the brain can be influenced by providing stimuli that increase the concentration of mediators stimulating neurogenesis. People are exposed to physical factors that can inhibit the neurogenesis process, but there are also phenomena that stimulate it. Magnetic stimulation, ultrasound, electrostimulation, light therapy, normobaric and hyperbaric oxygen therapy, whole-body cryotherapy, as well as touch and vibrations, can have a significant impact on neurogenesis and accelerate this process. The aim of this study is to present the impact of physical factors on the process of neurogenesis in humans and animals, which can significantly influence the course of this process. The review uses the wording originally used in the source articles.

articles.title: Thoracoabdominal Trauma in Disaster.
articles.journal_full: The Surgical clinics of North America

abstract.text: Disasters and mass casualty incidents overwhelm resources and force deviations from conventional care. Thoracoabdominal trauma involves 2 unforgiving compartments in which exsanguination, tension physiology, tamponade, and contamination are rapidly lethal. This article reviews the operational management of thoracic and abdominal injury when volume, personnel, and blood products are constrained. Topics include rapid recognition and decompression of tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, and cardiac tamponade; indications for damage control thoracic surgery, thoracic packing, temporary closure, and vascular shunting; hemorrhage and contamination control by retroperitoneal zone; and temporary abdominal closure options. Emphasis is placed on triage, resource stewardship, and deferring definitive reconstruction.

articles.title: Prehospital Triage and Transport During Mass Casualty Incidents and Disasters.
articles.journal_full: The Surgical clinics of North America

abstract.text: This article outlines a systems based approach to the EMS management of mass casualty incidents, emphasizing early recognition, escalation of resources, and coordinated communication. The article promotes Sort, Assess, Life-saving interventions, Treatment/Transport as the Model Uniform Core Criteria-compliant national triage standard, highlighting dynamic primary, secondary, and tertiary triage with ongoing retriage to minimize overtriage. It details the use of Casualty Collection Points and Ambulance Exchange Points, and underscores Incident Command System-structured, triage-driven transport led by a designated transport officer.

articles.title: Care of Special Populations in Disasters.
articles.journal_full: The Surgical clinics of North America

abstract.text: Disasters and mass casualty incidents disproportionately harm elderly, pediatric, and pregnant patients, yet most triage algorithms and preparedness plans are built around the healthy adult. This review examines the physiologic, anatomic, and social characteristics that make each population vulnerable, drawing on experience from Hurricane Katrina and contemporary armed conflict. For older adults, frailty, rather than chronologic age, drives outcomes, and polypharmacy complicates resuscitation. Children require age-adjusted triage, weight-based dosing, and protection from family separation. Pregnant patients require simultaneous maternal and fetal assessment, as the physiologic adaptations of pregnancy mask hemorrhage. Systems-level preparedness remains the strongest determinant of outcome.

articles.title: Impact of a Mentored Peer-Review Program on the Sponsoring Journal: Program Evaluation at Five Years.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The number of peer-reviewed biomedical journals has more than tripled over the past 20-25 years increasing the demand for quality peer reviewers. This demand and the lack of available formal training in peer review have resulted in a shortage of qualified peer reviewers. In response to this shortage, the Western Journal of Emergency Medicine Special Issue in Education (Special Issue) developed a formal mentored peer-review (MPR) program that provides a learning experience in peer review to educate fellows through legitimate participation while contributing to the editorial process of the journal. The latter serves as the basis of this study.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The impact of the MPR program on the Special Issue's reviewer pool served as the primary outcome of this study. This was accomplished by tracking the number of participating fellowships and their graduates who subsequently provided independent peer reviews for the sponsoring journal. Comparisons of MPRs generated by education fellows and their fellowship directors to those generated by our nonmentored faculty reviewers served two secondary outcomes: the quality of peer reviews and time from peer review offer to submission of the requisite peer reviews.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Over a period of five years, 82 fellows mentored by 43 fellowship directors submitted 147 MPRs. Of the 60 MPR graduates (35%), 21 were retained as independent peer reviewers. Based on a five-point editorial scoring scale (5 being excellent) mentored peer reviews received significantly higher editorial ratings (4.13 [SD 0.8]) than nonmentored faculty reviews (traditional reviewers) (3.33 [1.04]) and independent reviews by program graduates (3.61 [0.84]] (P < .001). We evaluated two peer-review turnaround periods. The first was the time from the initial two offers to review until two offers had been accepted. Instances where the first two offers were randomly made to MPRs were compared to offers to nonmentored faculty reviewers. The latter group took 60.2 (32.0) days compared to the MPR group, which averaged 17.2 (16.7) days (P < .001). The second interval measured the time from reviewer acceptance of the peer review until they submitted their completed review. There was no difference between the time in days between MPRs (10.4 [7.9]) and nonmentored faculty (9.4 [8.1]) in submitting reviews that had been accepted.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The mentored peer-review program contributed to increasing the Special Issue's reviewer pool with reviews of higher quality. In addition, by inviting two mentored peer-reviewers initially as compared to nonmentored faculty reviewers, the time frame for obtaining two secured peer-reviewers was significantly reduced. These findings demonstrate that a formalized approach to learning peer review by partnering with academically oriented fellowships has the potential to improve the availability of peer reviewers, the quality of peer reviews, and efficiency in the editorial review process.

articles.title: Management of late urinary side effects after pelvic radiation therapy: a scoping review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Radiation therapy (RT) is a cornerstone treatment for pelvic malignancies but can cause durable urinary side effects that impair quality of life. Presentations range from haematuria and irritative symptoms to stricture, fistula, osteomyelitis, and end-stage urinary failure. This scoping review maps the management strategies for late urinary side effects after pelvic RT.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A PRISMA-ScR-guided search of PubMed and Embase identified studies published from January 2015 to April 2026. Primary studies reporting management outcomes were included. Two reviewers assessed full-text eligibility. Data were charted by syndrome, intervention, design, population, RT characteristics, follow-up and outcomes. Risk of bias in randomised trials was assessed using RoB.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: 69 studies of previously irradiated patients were included, predominantly retrospective cohorts. RT modality was reported in 56% of publications, total dose in 33%, and the interval from RT to toxicity in 70%. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) had the strongest evidence for radiation cystitis, supported by randomised data and long-term follow-up. Reconstructive surgery for urethral and ureteral strictures achieved acceptable patency, but recurrence and incontinence remained common. Fistula, osteomyelitis, and refractory bleeding were often managed with salvage diversion in severe or refractory cases, which reduced pain and treatment burden despite substantial perioperative morbidity.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Evidence is strongest for HBOT in chronic radiation cystitis. Elsewhere, management rests on retrospective, expert-centre series. Clinical decision-making is best guided by syndrome, severity, and tissue quality, treating prior RT modality and dose as markers of injury burden, with timely referral and shared decision-making when repeated intervention fails to provide durable control.

articles.title: Infant carry sling-associated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and other circumstances surrounding such events in children under two years: A five-year regional registry analysis.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Infant carry slings are widely used for infant transport and bonding. However, concerns regarding safety have been raised, including risks of positional asphyxia from improper use, particularly in younger infants. This service evaluation explored the frequency of infant carry sling-associated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in children under two years old over a five-year period within a regional English ambulance service, placing these findings within the wider epidemiological context.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective observational service evaluation used data from an existing OHCA registry and included all patients aged under 2 years who received a resuscitation attempt following cardiac arrest between 1 April 2020 and 31 March 2025. Free-text narratives were reviewed to identify circumstances associated with OHCA, with particular attention paid to carry sling-associated OHCAs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 162 OHCA incidents in children aged under two years were identified, representing 1.0% of all resuscitation attempts during the five-year period. This included 114 infants aged under one year (excluding neonatal life support patients, n = 28). Only two carry sling-associated incidents were identified, both occurring in patients under one year, representing 1.8% of infant OHCAs. The most frequently documented circumstances surrounding OHCA were co-sleeping (33.3%) and patients found unresponsive (e.g. in a cot, bed, sofa or pushchair) (26.3%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Only two carry sling-associated OHCA incidents were identified over five years, suggesting such events were uncommon within this regional registry. In contrast, other sleep-related circumstances, particularly co-sleeping, accounted for a substantially larger proportion of infant OHCA cases.

articles.title: Quantifying discrepancies between EMS time intervals in the Swedish Registry for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and emergency medical dispatch data: a 10-year analysis.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To assess discrepancies between time intervals reported to the Swedish Registry for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (SRCR) for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) and those recorded by the dispatch centre between 2015 and 2024.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this retrospective observational study, OHCAs reported to the registry were linked to dispatch centre data to correct and validate EMS case numbers. Time interval discrepancies were quantified by comparing the EMS dispatch-to-arrival interval (unit response time) with the call start-to-arrival interval (total response time). Differences between the two sources were estimated using Bayesian quantile regression by modelling the median response-time distribution.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 56,969 registry records, 1004 (1.8%) lacked an EMS case number. On a pooled national level, unit response time showed negligible discrepancies between the two sources, with a median difference of 0.3 s (95% CrI -4.1 to 3.9). In contrast, the total response time was systematically shorter in the registry, with a median difference of -80.9 s (95% CrI -84.7 to -77.1). Both time intervals showed large regional variation, with the smallest difference in the Stockholm region.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: On a pooled national level, unit response time showed high concordance, whereas total response time was systematically shorter in the registry. Registry time variables, particularly total response time, should be interpreted with caution when evaluating small performance differences.

articles.title: Translation and validation of the TEAM-NL instrument for assessing interprofessional team performance in simulation-based resuscitation training.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Effective interprofessional teamwork is essential for successful resuscitation care. The Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) is widely used to assess emergency team performance; however, a validated Dutch version is lacking. This study aimed to translate and validate a Dutch version of the TEAM (TEAM-NL) for simulation-based resuscitation training.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A structured cross-cultural adaptation was performed, including forward-backward translation, developer review and expert review. Instructors used the TEAM-NL during Advanced Life Support courses at two Dutch training centres, rating each participant group in two simulation scenarios. Internal consistency, inter-rater reliability, convergent validity, change in scores between scenarios, acceptability and score distribution were assessed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 52 participant groups were observed, yielding 104 observed team performances and 299 instructor ratings. The mean total score (range 0-44) was 32.1 (SD 6.9). Internal consistency was high (Cronbach's α = 0.93). Inter-rater reliability was moderate for two raters (ICC(1,2) = 0.68, 95% CI 0.53-0.79) and good for three raters (ICC(1,3) = 0.78, 95% CI 0.69-0.85). The total score correlated strongly with the global performance rating (r = 0.86, p < 0.001). Scores were higher in the second scenario (mean difference 4.3, 95% CI 2.2-6.4; dz = 0.57). Missing data were minimal (0-2.7% per item). No floor effects were observed; ceiling effects were present for all items (19.4-36.1%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The TEAM-NL showed high internal consistency, convergent validity and acceptability for instructor-based assessment of team performance during simulation-based resuscitation training. Inter-rater reliability was moderate for two raters and good when the ratings of three instructors were averaged.

articles.title: Health and Emergency Preparedness for Mass Gatherings at the 2034 FIFA World Cup in Saudi Arabia: A Systematic Review and Targeted Evidence Update.

abstract.text: The Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) World Cups are complex mass gatherings that place simultaneous demands on public-health surveillance, environmental risk management, emergency medical services, crowd safety, and health-system resilience. Saudi Arabia's selection to host the 2034 tournament creates an opportunity to adapt capabilities developed through decades of Hajj operations to the very different context of a global football event. This review synthesises evidence from major mass gatherings and incorporates post-Qatar 2022 and World Cup 2026 evidence to define practical priorities for 2034. The original review searched PubMed, the Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE), Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for 2000-2025 and retained 43 records according to the documented screening log. A targeted update undertaken in September 2026 searched PubMed/MEDLINE and primary sources from major international, national, and sporting authorities. Because this update was not a complete rerun of the original four-database strategy, newer evidence was synthesised narratively and was not added to the original screening denominator. Post-Qatar studies support dedicated tournament medical services, improved clinician notification, open-source epidemic intelligence, and wastewater surveillance. World Cup 2026 evidence adds cross-jurisdictional dashboards, port-health surveillance, early-warning systems, pathogen-specific risk assessment, and multi-hazard environmental planning. Contemporary Saudi Hajj operations demonstrate large-scale heat prevention, surge care, referral, and emergency logistics. For Saudi Arabia 2034, the evidence favours an all-hazards model built around heat action plans, interoperable multi-layer surveillance, unified incident command, distributed emergency care, crowd-safety intelligence, mental-health pathways, multilingual communication, and predefined post-event evaluation. The central implementation principle is to strengthen routine national systems rather than construct temporary parallel systems for the tournament.

articles.title: Postpartum "Hypercoagulable Storm" With Extensive Iliocaval Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism in a Patient With Heterozygous Factor V Leiden.

abstract.text: A 26-year-old woman presented to the emergency department four weeks after a lower segment cesarean section with a four-day history of progressive dyspnea, bilateral lower limb swelling, and leg pain. At presentation to the emergency department, she was tachycardic (150 beats/min), hypotensive (88/60 mmHg), and tachypneic (38/min), with an oxygen saturation of 93% on room air. Venous Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated extensive bilateral deep vein thrombosis (DVT) involving the iliac veins, right external iliac vein, infrarenal inferior vena cava (IVC), and right popliteal vein, with left popliteal involvement. Computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography demonstrated acute pulmonary embolism (PE) involving the right pulmonary artery and multiple segmental branches, with right lower lobe pulmonary infarction. Thrombophilia evaluation identified heterozygous Factor V Leiden, with negative antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant and normal protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III levels. The initial presentation raised concern for high-risk acute pulmonary embolism physiology, with hypotension (88/60 mmHg), marked tachycardia, and respiratory compromise requiring high-flow oxygen. Category D1+R was considered provisionally; however, definitive classification was limited by the absence of documented hypotension duration and fluid responsiveness, lactate, echocardiographic right ventricular assessment, and computed tomography (CT) right ventricular (RV)/left ventricular (LV) ratio. A Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) was activated, and intravenous unfractionated heparin (UFH) was initiated. A retrievable suprarenal IVC filter was placed, followed by mechanical thrombectomy extending from the right popliteal vein to the IVC. At three months, the patient remained ambulatory without exertional dyspnea, and bilateral lower limb swelling had completely resolved. Repeat venous Doppler demonstrated recanalization of the previously thrombosed segments without significant residual occlusive thrombus. This case is presented because of the uncommon combination of extensive bilateral lower limb and iliocaval thrombosis with acute PE and pulmonary infarction in the early postpartum period in a patient with heterozygous Factor V Leiden. It highlights how postpartum hypercoagulability may interact with inherited thrombophilia to produce extensive multisite thrombosis and emphasizes the importance of early recognition, severity-based risk stratification, and coordinated multidisciplinary management.

articles.title: Point-of-Care Ultrasound Detection of Acute Myocardial Dysfunction Following Bupropion Overdose: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Bupropion overdose is associated with significant morbidity and mortality due to severe neurologic and cardiovascular toxicity, including seizures and life-threatening arrhythmias. Early recognition of electrocardiographic, clinical, and echocardiographic abnormalities is critical for prompt intervention and prevention of clinical deterioration. We present a case of a 21-year-old female who presented to the emergency department following an intentional polysubstance overdose involving suspected bupropion ingestion. The initial electrocardiogram (EKG) demonstrated sinus tachycardia. However, during continued monitoring, the patient developed QRS widening and seizures. Treatment included benzodiazepines, calcium, and sodium bicarbonate. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) revealed a reduced ejection fraction (EF) of less than 30%, which was later confirmed on formal transthoracic echocardiography. These findings prompted escalation of care, intubation for airway protection and deep sedation, and transfer to the intensive care unit (ICU). During admission, she developed torsades de pointes (TdP), resulting in cardiac arrest. Despite her critical presentation, repeat echocardiography upon resolution of overdose toxicity demonstrated recovery of left ventricular systolic function, with improvement of EF to 50-55% during hospitalization. This case demonstrates the potential role of POCUS in the early recognition of myocardial dysfunction associated with bupropion toxicity. Together with serial EKG monitoring, these findings identified a patient at high risk for clinical deterioration and supported early escalation of care.

articles.title: Clinical and laboratory characteristics associated with in-hospital mortality in methanol poisoning: A 5-year retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To compare the demographic, clinical, and laboratory characteristics of survivors and non-survivors presenting to the emergency department with methanol poisoning and to identify variables associated with in-hospital mortality.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This single-center retrospective observational cohort study included all consecutive adults (≥18 years) diagnosed with methanol poisoning at the emergency department of Giresun Training and Research Hospital, Türkiye, between September 01, 2021, and May 01, 2026. Patients were categorized as survivors and non-survivors. Demographic characteristics, clinical findings, laboratory parameters, severity scores (Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS], Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II [APACHE II], and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment [SOFA]), and treatment variables were compared using univariable analyses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 26 patients were included, and 9 (34.6%) died. At emergency department presentation, loss of consciousness was more frequent among non-survivors (88.9% vs. 11.8%; p<0.001). Non-survivors also had lower GCS scores (median 4 vs. 15; p<0.001) and admission pH (7.00 vs. 7.11; p=0.011), together with higher lactate (7.1 vs. 2.9 mmol/L; p<0.001), creatinine (1.52 vs. 1.00 mg/dL; p=0.001), glucose (194 vs. 123 mg/dL; p=0.029), and anion gap levels (27.0 vs. 20.9 mmol/L; p=0.018). Within the intensive care unit (ICU) subgroup (n=20), ICU non-survivors (n=9) had higher APACHE II and SOFA scores than ICU survivors (n=11) (p=0.002 and p<0.001, respectively). During the subsequent hospital course, all non-survivors required invasive mechanical ventilation compared with none of the survivors (100% vs. 0%; p<0.001); this finding was considered a marker of greater clinical severity rather than a baseline prognostic characteristic.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this small exploratory cohort, non-survivors showed greater neurological impairment and a general pattern of more severe metabolic derangement at emergency department presentation. Within the selected ICU subgroup, ICU non-survivors had higher APACHE II and SOFA scores than ICU survivors. These findings are hypothesis-generating and may help identify clinical features warranting heightened concern; however, they should not be interpreted as validated prognostic criteria or as a risk-stratification tool.

articles.title: [AI-manipulated medical records as part of medical child abuse].

abstract.text: This case report describes a rare case of Medical Child Abuse (MCA) where AI-manipulated videos were used to fabricate seizures. A two-year-old boy was admitted to a pediatric emergency department under suspicion of epilepsy after his mother reported frequent seizures. During a five-day hospitalisation, the mother described two daily seizures, only witnessed by her. To substantiate the seizures, she presented three videos. Normal clinical findings and suspicious video footage led to concerns of MCA. When confronted, the mother admitted using generative AI tools to create the videos.

articles.title: Sex Differences in Outcome and Mortality in Urinary Tract Infections in the Emergency Department: The UTILY Study.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: In urinary tract infections (UTI) sex-related differences in comorbidities, antimicrobial resistance, and outcomes have been described, but it remains unclear whether these disparities reflect sex-related biological mechanisms or are primarily explained by age and comorbidity, especially in emergency settings. Our objective was to evaluate sex-related differences in microbiology, antimicrobial resistance, and outcomes among adults with potentially multidrug-resistant UTIs presenting to the emergency department (ED), and to determine whether sex independently predicts multidrug-resistant infections and outcomes after adjustment for age and comorbidity.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a prospective multicenter study enrolling all adult patients with suspected or confirmed UTIs admitted to one of the eight EDs involved from February 2023-July 2024. Our primary outcome was the prevalence of multidrug-resistant UTIs and whether sex independently predicted multidrug-resistant infection after adjustment for age and comorbidity. Secondary outcomes included hospitalization, adequacy of empirical antibiotic therapy, clinical response at 7 days, and 7-day and 30-day all-cause mortality. Demographic, clinical, and microbiological data were compared by sex. To account for baseline differences in age and comorbidity burden (Charlson Comorbidity Index), multivariable logistic regression models were applied to identify independent predictors of multidrug-resistant infection, hospitalization, and 30-day mortality.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We included 679 patients (358 males, 321 females). Mean age was 70.1 years (standard deviation 17.9) in males and 63.1 years (21.4) in females (P < .001). The Charlson Comorbidity Index was higher in males (2.50 [2.45]) than in females (1.85 [2.32]) (P = .01). Multidrug-resistant infection occurred in 107/321 females (33.5%) and 166/358 males (46.5%) (P = .02). Adequate empirical therapy was achieved in 213/321 females (66.2%) and 221/358 males (61.8%) (P = .10). Hospitalization occurred in 176/321 females (54.9%) and 175/358 males (48.8%) (P = .09). Seven-day mortality was 14/321 females (4.5%) and 28/358 males (7.9%) (P = .05), while 30-day mortality was 32/321 females (9.9%) and 50/358 males (14.0%) (P = .05). After adjustment for age and comorbidity, male sex remained independently associated with multidrug-resistant infection (adjusted odds ratio 1.45; 95% CI, 1.03-2.10, P sex = .02; P age = .01).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Male sex was independently associated with multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections in the emergency department, even after adjustment for age and comorbidity. These findings highlight the need for sex- and risk-based approaches to empirical therapy and antimicrobial stewardship in acute care settings.

articles.title: Purple Haze as a Tell-Tale Sign: A Case Report.

abstract.text: Patients with urinary tract infection (UTI) symptoms report dysuria, urinary frequency, fever, and/or urinary urgency. In addition, those with catheter-associated UTIs may have flank pain or suprapubic or costovertebral tenderness. We present a case of a rare physical examination finding that can also aid in the diagnosis of a catheter-associated UTI: purple urine bag syndrome (PUBS). An 84-year-old man with a past medical history of metastatic prostate cancer complicated by a rectourethral fistula, status post ileal conduit and loop colostomy, presented after his daughter noticed what she believed was blood in the overnight drainage bag connected to his ileal conduit. The patient had previously required bilateral percutaneous nephrostomy tubes for malignant extrinsic ureteral compression from progressive prostate cancer, but the right nephrostomy tube had subsequently been removed after identifying that the left-sided obstruction was the culprit. The patient was reporting right-sided abdominal pain and fatigue. On examination, the patient was lethargic and unable to provide a history. Examination revealed dark purple discoloration of the ileal conduit tubing and overnight drainage bag. A Foley catheter placed by the emergency department did not drain urine because of the patient's ileal conduit and was subsequently removed. Urinalysis did not demonstrate hematuria, indicating that the discoloration perceived as blood was the purple hue shown in the clinical photograph. Urine specimens were obtained from the functioning urinary drainage sites, and the culture obtained from the ileal conduit collection bag was positive. The patient was started on ertapenem and daptomycin due to a history of severe sepsis secondary to vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) UTI from his ileal conduit and extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing (ESBL) Escherichia coli from his catheter site. CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated hydronephrosis of the right kidney with concern for developing pyelonephritis. The right-sided hydronephrosis was attributed to malignant extrinsic ureteral compression from progressive prostate cancer. The urine culture from the ileal conduit collection bag grew Providencia stuartii, Proteus mirabilis, E. coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, all of which were susceptible to meropenem. Due to concern for pyelonephritis and a rise in the patient's creatinine, a right-sided percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) tube was placed, and the patient's condition improved after a six-day course of meropenem. This case is notable for purple discoloration of the ileal conduit tubing and overnight collection bag, consistent with PUBS. This syndrome is associated with UTIs in elderly people, particularly those who are constipated. The source of the pigment has been attributed to altered tryptophan metabolism related to prolonged intestinal transit time and the production of indole derivatives by bacteria. The tryptophan metabolites produce red and blue pigments that combine to form the purple color seen in PUBS. In this patient, the culture obtained from the ileal conduit collection bag grew predominantly Providencia stuartii and Proteus mirabilis, both of which have been implicated in this syndrome. The patient's right-sided hydronephrosis occurred in the setting of malignant extrinsic ureteral compression from progressive prostate cancer rather than obstruction of the bladder or urethra.

articles.title: Machine Learning Algorithms for Predicting Psychostimulant Intoxication in Emergency Department Patients: A Multicenter Study.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Psychostimulant detection rates among emergency department (ED) patients presenting with suspected substance intoxication are low and are influenced by limited access to confirmatory testing, insufficient clinical information, and variability in physician experience. These challenges often result in high false-positive rates and unnecessary resource use. We hypothesized that machine learning (ML) algorithms could maintain reliable diagnostic performance across a temporal validation cohort and perform comparably to physicians with varying experience levels.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This multicenter study prospectively enrolled ED patients with suspected substance intoxication between March 2019 and January 2020. We chronologically partitioned data into a training set (March-October 2019) and a temporal validation cohort (November 2019-January 2020) to assess model generalizability. After determining psychostimulant intoxication via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry from urine samples, we trained the ML algorithms using the confirmed positive cases. The primary outcome was the diagnostic discrimination of the models, measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) in the temporal validation cohort. Secondary outcomes included model accuracy, the Youden index, and a comparative assessment of sensitivity and specificity relative to five physicians of varying experience levels.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 1,382 patients (mean age 43.8 [standard deviation 19.2] years; 55.3% male), 302 patients (21.9%) had confirmed psychostimulant intoxication, primarily involving (meth)amphetamines (134 [44.4%]), cathinones (107 [35.4%]), and ketamine (97 [32.1%]). In the temporal validation cohort (n = 382), the ML models demonstrated consistent performance, with AUCs ranging from 0.786 to 0.836. The primary outcome was met by the top-performing extreme gradient boosting (XGB) model (AUC, 0.836, 95% CI, 0.785-0.882; accuracy, 0.866 (95% CI, 0.838-0.895); and Youden index, 0.590 (95% CI, 0.480-0.694). To evaluate secondary outcomes, the XGB model's predictive accuracy was evaluated against 5 emergency physicians. The model surpassed the junior emergency physicians in both specificity (0.910 vs 0.633-0.867) and sensitivity (0.681 vs 0.500-0.633); its specificity was comparable to that of the senior emergency physicians (0.900-0.933).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Machine learning models provide reliable diagnostic utility for identifying psychostimulant intoxication, achieving performance comparable to senior emergency physicians. While moderate sensitivity (0.389-0.708) limits their role as standalone rule-out tools, their high specificity provides a standardized tool to assist clinical decision-making and reduce diagnostic uncertainty in the fast-paced ED setting.

articles.title: Identification of Regional Wall Motion Abnormalities by Emergency Physicians in Acute Coronary Syndromes: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Chest pain accounts for approximately six million emergency department (ED) visits annually in the United States. Early detection of acute occlusive myocardial infarction (OMI) is challenging, especially in patients without classic ST-elevation on initial electrocardiography (ECG). Regional wall motion abnormalities (RWMA) often precede ECG changes and can be sensitive indicators of acute coronary occlusion on transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). However, the accuracy of emergency physician-performed TTE for RWMA detection has not been well defined. In this review we aim to determine how accurate emergency physicians are in detecting RWMAs.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a systematic review of studies including adult ED patients who underwent cardiac ultrasound performed or interpreted by emergency physicians, with test characteristics compared to cardiology-performed or interpreted echocardiography as the reference standard. Primary outcomes were sensitivity and specificity for RWMA detection. Secondary outcomes included likelihood ratios, and area under the receiver-operator curve (AUC). Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2, and evidence certainty was evaluated using GRADE methodology.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The search identified 2,463 studies, of which 32 underwent full-text review; nine studies including 1,191 participants from the US, Turkey, and Iran are included. Sonographers across studies ranged from medical students and residents to fellowship-trained and senior emergency physicians with varying levels of prior ultrasound and RWMA-specific training. Pooled sensitivity and specificity for RWMA detection were 86% (95% CI, 76-93%) and 85% (95% CI, 70-94%), respectively, with an AUC of 0.918. Pooled positive and negative likelihood ratios were 5.42 (95% CI, 2.51-11.68) and 0.17 (95% CI, 0.09-0.33), respectively. Four of the nine studies were judged to have a high risk of bias in at least one domain. Substantial heterogeneity was observed in the secondary univariate analyses (>80%). The overall certainty of evidence was moderate.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Emergency physician-performed or interpreted cardiac ultrasound demonstrates high accuracy for detecting RWMAs compared with cardiology-performed or interpreted echocardiography. Although heterogeneity was observed across studies, the overall certainty of evidence was moderate. Structured training and standardized protocols may optimize diagnostic performance.

articles.title: Ethics of Medical Students as Embedded Simulation Participants in Ultrasound Education.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Medical students are sometimes used as embedded simulation participants (ESP) to facilitate ultrasound training on live volunteers. There is little guidance on how to safeguard the autonomy and dignity of medical student ESPs serving in this role. Based on real student experiences, we used four cases to illustrate the ethical dilemmas that can arise when ESPs are used, including the examination of sensitive body areas, risk for coercion, discovery of incidental findings in a public and professional setting, and social media posting of training events. Through these cases, we explore and articulate the relevant ethical obligations educators have to obtain informed consent, sensitively address incidental findings, and ensure the psychological and physical safety of ESPs.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We developed interventions and procedures at our institution to address the obligation to promote ESP autonomy and bodily dignity, including a comprehensive consent form, ombudsperson role, and restrictions surrounding photography and social media posting of educational events.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: These interventions were implemented in January 2024 in the emergency department of a large academic medical center affiliated with a medical school. Since implementation, 96 ESPs have participated in 16 discrete educational events. There has been anecdotal positive reception of these interventions. Recruiting and training individuals for the ombudsperson role carried some challenges.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Proactive measures are necessary to support the autonomy and safety of medical student ESPs. There are practical challenges associated with recruitment, training, and implementation of the ombudsperson role. We hope that other institutions who use medical student ESPs will consider incorporating similar practices to promote the psychological and bodily safety of their volunteers.

articles.title: Impact of Away Rotations on Emergency Medicine Match Rates in the Virtual Residency Recruitment Era.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, many emergency medicine (EM) residencies have transitioned to virtual interviews, providing less in-person exposure for applicants. Away rotations offer applicants the opportunity to gain in-person exposure to residency programs beyond the virtual interview environment. Whether the away rotation is more important now and leads to higher rotator match rates in the virtual recruitment era remains unclear and warrants investigation. Our objective was to determine the percentage of EM interns who completed an in-person rotation at the residency program in which they matched and compare this to pre-COVID-19 match rates.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a multicenter pilot study of EM residency programs. We recruited a convenience sample of academic programs from the eight Society for Academic Emergency Medicine (SAEM) US geographic regions. Inclusion criteria included academic EM programs that conducted virtual-only interviews post-COVID-19. We collected data via a survey form for the 2017-2024 application years regarding the number of matched interns who completed an in-person rotation at the program and the number of matched interns who were "home" versus "away" rotators. The first three years were defined as pre-COVID and the last three as post-COVID. The 2020-2021 academic year was excluded given the elimination of most away rotations during this cycle. We compared proportions of matched interns before and after COVID-19.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eleven of 13 invited programs (representing seven of eight SAEM regions) participated in our analysis. Pre-COVID, 95 of 384 interns (24.7%; 95% CI, 20.5-29.4%) completed a rotation at their respective residency program. Post-COVID, this decreased by 2.86% (absolute risk difference; 95% CI, -6.13% to 4.02%; McNemar's P = .06) to 84 of 384 (21.9%; 95% CI, 17.8-26.3%). Focusing solely on "away" rotators, 48 of the matched interns (12.5%; 95% CI, 9.4-16.2%) completed a rotation at their residency program pre-COVID compared to 47 interns (12.2%; 95% CI, 9.1-15.9%) post-COVID (P = .82). The absolute risk difference for the away rotators was 0.7% (95% CI, -10.6% to 9.1%, P = .82).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this pilot study, we found no statistically significant difference in the proportion of matched interns who completed an in-person rotation in the pre- versus post-COVID-19 era.

articles.title: Emergency Ultrasound Fellowship Match Outcomes: Unfilled Positions and Implications over Eight Years.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Advanced emergency ultrasound (AEMUS) fellowships recently experienced an unexpected decrease in the number of positions filled in the match. Our study aimed to characterize this trend over an eight-year period.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a cross-sectional observational study of AEMUS fellowships participating in the National Resident Matching Program (NRMP) from the 2019-2026 match cycles, cross-referencing the publicly available database from the Society of Clinical Ultrasound Fellowships. The primary outcome was both the proportion of AEMUS fellowship positions filled and a program complement fill percentage. Secondary outcomes included stratification by geography and duration since program establishment.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We included a total of 138 of the 141 programs listed in the NRMP Match. From 2019 to 2026, there was a 28.2% increase in the number of programs and a 34.5% increase in available positions. There was a general increase in the percentage of positions filled from 2019 to 2022, with 53.7% (87/162) of positions filled to 74.4% (145/195), peaking at 81.1% (137/169) in 2021. This upward trend reversed in 2023 with a decrease to 65.1% (142/218). The percentage of positions filled has continued to decrease through 2026, with a fill rate of only 56.0% (122/218). In the eight years of NRMP data, 97 of the 138 programs (70.3%) went unfilled at least once. Programs participating in the Match for a longer period had a statistically significant higher fill percentage, with 27 programs in the 1- to 4-year group with a total fill percentage of 46.0%, 32 programs in the 5- to 7-year group with a fill percentage of 59.0%, and 79 programs in the ≥ 8-year group with a fill percentage of 72.8% (P < .01) using a Kruskal-Wallis test. Spearman correlation analysis found no association between geographic proximity and likelihood of a program being fully filled.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This cross-sectional study of NRMP data showed a decrease in the percentage of positions filled for adult AEMUS fellowships starting in 2023, which continued through 2026. Programs with greater longevity exhibited higher fill percentages, showing resilience in the face of this pattern.

articles.title: High-efficiency Nebulizers Reduce Albuterol Administration Time in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Asthma exacerbations commonly require nebulized albuterol in the emergency department (ED). High-efficiency devices (vibrating mesh, breath-enhanced/actuated) may shorten treatment time compared with traditional jet nebulizers. We compared four commonly used nebulizer devices on treatment time and ED outcomes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a prospective observational study of a convenience sample of patients at a high-volume, urban Level I trauma center ED (February 2019-March 2023; paused during COVID-19). Patients ≥ 3 years of age receiving clinician-ordered nebulized albuterol were eligible. Exclusions included patients with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or congestive heart failure, inability to follow commands or hold the device, and need for positive-pressure ventilation. Respiratory care practitioners used one of four devices already in use in this department: Westmed miniHEART Hi-Flo jet (Mini), Aerogen Ultra (vibrating mesh), Monaghan AeroEclipse II (breath-actuated), or Salter Labs NebuTech (breath-enhanced). The Mini group received a single 15-mg dose; others received 5-mg increments up to 15 mg with reassessment. Our primary outcome measure was the shortest time to complete delivery of the planned albuterol dose to the patient. Secondary outcomes included hospital admission and changes in asthma security scores and peak expiratory flow. We used analysis of variance post-hoc tests and adjusted linear/logistic regression. Both males and females were included; sex-stratified analyses were not prespecified.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We enrolled 296 patients (Mini, n = 90; Aerogen, n = 67; AeroEclipse, n = 65; NebuTech, n = 74), 78 (26.3%) of whom were pediatric patients 3-18 years of age (Mini, n = 22; Aerogen, n = 20; AeroEclipse, n = 14, and NebuTech, n = 22). Time to complete albuterol differed by device, with mean treatment times in minutes (95% CI): Mini, 60.6 [55.9-65.3]; Aerogen, 12.3 [10.9-13.7]; AeroEclipse, 8.7 [7.7-9.7]; and NebuTech, 7.9 [7.0-8.8]. Adjusted models showed 82%, 88%, and 88% relative reductions vs Mini (all P < .01). Admission rates did not differ in total percentage (Mini, 11.1 [10]; Aerogen, 14.9 [10]; AeroEclipse, 16.9 [11]; and NebuTech, 6.8 [5] (all P > .05). Adults had lower odds of admission than pediatrics (odds ratio 0.38; 95% CI, 0.18-0.79; P = .01), with a total of 36 (12.1%) patients requiring admission, two pediatric. Asthma severity and improvements in peak expiratory flow were similar across devices, with mean post-treatment values (asthma severity score and peak expiratory flow): Mini, 5.5 and 301.1; Aerogen, 5.6 and 292.7; AeroEclipse, 5.9 and 248.5; and NebuTech, 5.7 and 301.1 (all P > .01).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In a real-world ED cohort, vibrating-mesh and breath-enhanced/actuated nebulizers delivered albuterol > 80% faster than a traditional jet device, potentially saving at least 45 minutes per treatment per patient, without differences in admission rates or clinical response. Adopting faster devices may improve workflow and throughput without compromising patient outcomes.

articles.title: Pediatric Unspecified Headache in the Emergency Department: Can We Do Better?
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Unspecified headache is a common discharge diagnosis in the pediatric emergency department (ED). While diagnostic uncertainty and limited access to specialty evaluation may contribute to repeat ED visits in this population, longitudinal utilization data are limited. Study objectives were both to determine the incidence of repeat headache-related ED visits in children discharged from the ED with unspecified headache and to identify predictors of ED return (eg, prior headache-related ED or neurology utilization).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This preliminary, prospective longitudinal cohort study included 76 children (ages 8-17 years) discharged from the ED with an unspecified headache diagnosis. We assessed headache-related ED and outpatient neurology visits both six months after the index visit (ie, ED enrollment) and, retrospectively, 12 months before the index visit. The sample included children insured through a Medi-Cal-based Physician-Hospital Consortium, who receive care exclusively within an integrated healthcare network, and other children in the hospital network, allowing capture of all ED and clinic utilization data. Our primary outcome was incidence of headache-related ED utilization postindex visit. Pain characteristics were self-reported during the index visit. Chi-square, Mann-Whitney U, and logistic regression analyses examined factors associated with incidence of headache-related ED returns.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Nearly 12% (n = 9) of children returned to the ED for a headache 6 months following the index visit. Across the 18-month study, 22.4% had at least one headache-related ED visit outside the index visit, 64.7% (n = 11) of whom had ≥2 headache-related ED encounters. A prior headache-related ED visit or prior neurology visit was significantly associated with returning to the ED after the index visit (20.0% vs 3.0%; risk difference = 17.0%; 95% CI, 0.9%-48.0%; P = .03, and 37.5% vs 1.5%; risk difference = 28.7%; 95% CI, 3.2%-60.9%; P = .02, respectively). Children with more than two headache-related ED visits during the 18-month study reported higher pain intensity (7.00 [SD, 1.38] vs 5.79 [SD, 2.09]; mean difference = -1.21; 95% CI, -2.20 to -0.22; P = .02). In logistic regression analyses, prior neurology utilization was the only variable significantly associated with headache-related ED return (OR, 15.31; 95% CI, 1.08-216.34; P = .04).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: A considerable proportion of children discharged with unspecified headache returned to the ED for headache. Emergency department and neurology utilization and pain intensity were linked to return ED visits. Larger, longitudinal studies are needed to further clarify these findings.

articles.title: Normative Distal Radius Radiological Measurements: The Influence of Age, Gender, and Menopause.
articles.journal: Clin Med Insights Arthritis Musculoskelet Disord
articles.journal_full: Clinical medicine insights. Arthritis and musculoskeletal disorders

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Distal radius fractures are prevalent, with management dependent on accurate radiological assessment. Most morphologic reference values derive from Western cohorts, raising questions about their generalizability. This study established reference distal radius radiological parameters in the Israeli population derived from emergency department patients with non-fractured wrist injuries and explored the effects of age, gender, and menopause.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective review included adults with wrist contusions at an Israeli emergency department. Exclusions were prior fractures, surgery, or poor radiographs.
